title: Orientation
text: Before any code: what data is, and how to use this course

title: Data is everywhere (you make it right now)
text:
Every tap, step and swipe writes a record. A data analyst turns raw records into answers and decisions.
Data is just facts stored as text and numbers: "Ana", 42, "2026-09-18 14:03". The analyst's job: ask the right question, pull the records that answer it, and check the answer is believable.
A record (row) describes one thing — one customer, one order, one sensor ping.
A field (column) is one kind of fact about that thing — name, amount, timestamp.
Big questions ("why did revenue dip?") are answered from tiny facts.
If it can't be measured and written down, a computer can't count it.

title: What a data analyst actually does
text:
A fixed pipeline, every single time: question → data → clean → analyze → show → decide.
Every analytics project — a $10 dashboard or a billion-dollar fraud model — walks this same line. Watch it below. Nothing in this course ever leaves this pipeline; each later phase is one station of it, zoomed in.
The question decides everything else — a sharp question saves weeks of work.
Cleaning is usually 50–80% of the effort; plan for it, don't pretend.
The deliverable is a decision, not a chart. Charts are the argument.
If any station lies, the decision lies — that's why every step is checkable.

title: How to use this course (60-second version)
text:
Every step follows the same rhythm: read one idea, play the motion, touch the controls, answer one question.
This course has
Green box = real-life version of the idea. Read it first — it's the anchor.
Play / ▶ buttons = the motion. Always press them once; the animation is the explanation.
Sliders & clicks on the canvas = your turn. Break things on purpose.
Answer the question, read the why, then press Next. One step = one idea, nothing more.

title: SQL — the language of data
text: Tables, filters, joins, indexes, transactions — how data is stored and asked questions

title: Tables: rows are things, columns are facts
text:
Almost every system on Earth — banks, Netflix, hospitals — stores data in tables: named columns of facts, one row per thing.
Each row is a record; each column a field with one type (text, number, date). Click column headers below to sort, and click any cell to pin it. Types matter: a price of "19.99" (text) can't be summed by the machine — it will silently skip it.
Row = record: one customer, one order, one ping.
Column = field: one kind of fact, one type (text / number / date).
Duplicate rows are allowed unless you say otherwise (unique constraint).
Every serious database can be read this way — SQL is the shared language on top.

title: WHERE — keep only the rows you asked for
text: A table answers "everything". A question is almost always about a subset — WHERE is how you name that subset. WHERE compares each row and keeps the ones that pass. Combine conditions with AND (both must pass), OR (one is enough), NOT (invert). Toggle conditions below and watch rows disappear. WHERE runs row by row: pass → keep, fail → drop. AND is stricter (smaller result); OR is looser (bigger result). IS NULL tests for missing — = NULL would never work (missing ≠ equal to anything). Big tables: WHERE is also where performance lives — the engine can skip most rows if you write it well (see indexes).

title: GROUP BY + aggregates — from rows to answers
text:
"How much did each city spend?" — GROUP BY piles rows into buckets; aggregates (SUM, AVG, COUNT) give each bucket one number.
Rule that trips everyone: every column you show must either be grouped or aggregated. If you ask "name, city, SUM(amount)" — which Ana? The engine refuses, and it's right. Click a city bucket to see its rows fold in.
GROUP BY city → one row per city; the rest must go through SUM/AVG/COUNT/MIN/MAX.
HAVING filters after grouping ("cities with SUM > 100"); WHERE filters rows before.
COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(col) skips missing values — often a data-quality tell.
This one pattern (bucket → summarize) is 80% of business reporting.

title: JOINs — combining two tables on a shared key
text:
A name lives in one table, the address in another. JOINs stitch rows together where a key matches — the single most-used operation in analytics.
Both tables must share a key (here id). Pick a join type below and watch which row pairs survive. NULL (red) means "no match found, but keep me anyway."
INNER: only pairs that match — the default, the safest.
LEFT: keep every left row; unmatched ones get NULLs (great for finding orphans).
RIGHT/FULL: mirror images — keep the other side too. FULL keeps everything on both sides.
CROSS: every row × every row (n×m) — a deliberate explosion, rarely wanted.

title: CTEs & subqueries — answer in stages
text: Hard questions are two easy ones. A CTE (WITH x AS (…)) names the first answer, then the second question builds on it. Watch the two stages below. Stage 1 computes "top spender per city"; stage 2 asks a question about those winners only. Without the CTE you'd repeat the whole stage-1 computation inside stage 2 — or worse, get it subtly different. WITH winners AS (…) = "pretend this table exists"; use it by name afterwards. CTEs can reference earlier CTEs — a chain of named stages. Subqueries do the same inside a SELECT/WHERE; CTEs are usually more readable. Each stage is independently checkable — that's the debugging superpower.

title: Window functions — rank & running totals without collapsing
text: GROUP BY crushes rows into one per bucket. Window functions do the math alongside the rows — each row keeps its identity, plus a computed badge. RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY cat ORDER BY time) ranks within each category. SUM(x) OVER (ORDER BY t) gives a running total. Click a category below to spotlight its ranking. PARTITION BY = buckets that never merge rows (unlike GROUP BY). ORDER BY inside OVER() decides the ranking / running order. row_number (unique), rank (gaps on ties), dense_rank (no gaps) — pick by tie policy. Running totals + RANK = the tool behind 90% of "leaderboard" dashboards.

title: Indexes & B-trees — why "WHERE id=42" is instant
text:
A table with no index is a stack of papers — every search reads everything. An index is a layered signpost: a few hops, then done.
A B-tree keeps keys sorted on each level; each hop narrows the search to ~1/n of the rest. Press ▶ to search for 42 and watch the hop count (right) stay at 3 while the linear scan (below) crawls row by row.
Linear scan = O(n): 10M rows → up to 10M comparisons.
B-tree search = O(log n): 10M rows → ~24 comparisons, same every time.
Indexes cost space and slow down INSERT/UPDATE (they must be kept in sync).
One index per queried column is not the answer — the optimizer picks; over-indexing backfires.

title: Transactions & ACID — the bank transfer promise
text:
"Move €50 from Ana to Ben" is two writes. If the machine dies between them, money is created or destroyed. A transaction makes that impossible.
Play the transfer. On step 3 the bank "crashes" (toggle it on before playing) — watch ROLLBACK restore both balances, or COMMIT bank the change. Atomic, Consistent, Isolated, Durable — four words, one promise.
Atomic: all-or-nothing — the unit of all-or-nothing is the transaction.
Consistent: every rule (total money is constant) holds before and after.
Isolated: two transfers at once don't see each other's half-states.
Durable: after COMMIT, even a crash can't take the money back.

title: Normalization — don't store the same fact twice
text:
If the department manager's name sits in 200 employee rows, one promotion means 200 edits — and the 199 you forget are now lies.
Left: one table where dept_manager repeats on every employee row (3rd normal form violation). Click the manager's name — every dependent row that must be edited at once lights up. Right: the manager moves to its own table; employees keep a tiny dept_id foreign key.
1NF: one value per cell, no repeating groups.
2NF: no partial dependence (a fact about the dept must not live in a row keyed by employee+dept).
3NF: no transitive dependence — dept → manager is a dept fact, store it with the dept.
Foreign keys (dept_id) are the glue: small, typed, unambiguous.

title: Thinking with data
text: Descriptive stats, probability, inference — the logic behind every number

title: Mean, median, mode — three centers, three stories
text:
"Average" hides three different ideas. Which one you use changes the story — sometimes on purpose.
Mean = everything pooled and split evenly (sensitive to extremes). Median = the middle row (robust). Mode = the most common value. Add the CEO below and watch the two lines diverge.
Mean is a balance point — outliers drag it.
Median is a crowd middle — add any number of outliers, it barely moves.
Mode is the typical case — best for categories (most popular size, color).
Reporting "the average" without saying which is how numbers lie politely.

title: Spread: standard deviation — how wild is the data?
text:
Two waiters average the same tips (€15). One is boringly reliable; the other is a slot machine. The average can't tell them apart — spread can.
Standard deviation (σ) = "typical distance from the average." The ±1σ band holds ~68% of normal data. Slide the variability and watch the same average look completely different.
σ answers "how surprised should I be?" — small σ = predictable.
Variance = σ² — same information, squared (used inside formulas).
For normal data: ~68% of values within mean±1σ, ~95% within mean±2σ.
IQR (middle 50%) is the robust cousin when outliers distort σ.

title: Distribution shape — click to build it yourself
text: A distribution is just a crowd of numbers, sorted into a skyline. Its shape (center, spread, tails) is the story. Click the canvas to add random values (blue = first worker, pink = second). Load the income preset and flip the "normal overlay" to see the fit. Watch the mean (red) and median (green) as your shape changes. Symmetric bell ≈ normal — mean = median, σ does the talking. Right skew: mean > median (a long right tail drags the mean). Left skew: mean < median. Tails = risk: heavy tails mean "what usually happens" hides rare, huge events.

title: Correlation vs causation — the ice-cream trap
text:
Ice-cream sales and shark attacks rise and fall together, r ≈ 0.9. Eating ice cream does not summon sharks. A third thing — summer heat — drives both.
Three presets below: a real link (study time → grades), a confounded link (ice cream ↔ sharks), and pure noise. Click the canvas to add your own points and watch r move. Strong r never proves cause — it only says "look, they're connected."
r ranges −1…+1: strength AND direction of a linear link.
r=0.9 says nothing about cause, direction, or a hidden third variable.
Classic confounders: season, population size, "more stores of X" = "more people buying X".
The escape hatches: controlled experiments (A/B tests) or carefully argued mechanisms.

title: Sampling & the law of large numbers
text:
You can't taste the whole ocean — you taste a spoonful. Sampling works when the sample is random, and the bigger the spoonful, the closer it gets to the truth.
A fair coin: truth = 50% heads. Play flips and watch the running proportion wobble wildly at first, then settle. Slide the sample size and see how the 95% "confidence band" tightens around the truth.
Random = every unit has a chance — that's what makes the math honest.
Small samples wobble: with n=10, 8 heads (80%) is normal noise, not a biased coin.
Large samples settle: the band shrinks like 1/√n.
Non-random samples can be wrong at ANY size — the math only rescues randomness.

title: Probability: binomial & Poisson — counting rare events
text:
Probability is just "how often would I see this if the world worked the way I think it does?" Two workhorses: binomial (fixed tries) and Poisson (rare arrivals).
Left: binomial bars P(exactly k successes) with n tries and per-try probability p. Slide both. Right: Poisson for arrivals with average λ per window. These curves are how SREs size on-call and how insurers price risk.
Binomial: fixed n independent tries, each success prob p. The bars always sum to 1.
The binomial peak sits near n·p — "expected value = n × p".
Poisson: counts of rare, independent arrivals in a window; λ = average count.
"Rare × many chances" = surprisingly common: 1% failure × 1,000 requests ≈ 63% chance of ≥1 failure.

title: Confidence intervals & hypothesis testing — "is this real?"
text:
Every measurement is truth + noise. A confidence interval is an honest shrug with bounds: "the effect is in this range, 95 times out of 100."
Below: the truth slider sets reality (0 = the pill does nothing). Each ▶ run measures 30 patients and reports the observed effect, its 95% CI, and the verdict. Set truth to 0 and run 10 times — you'll watch ~5 "false alarms" happen purely by luck. That's the 5% error rate everyone agrees to accept.
95% CI: build it 100 times, ~95 will cover the true value. (It's about the method, not one interval.)
p < 0.05: "if nothing were real, this result would happen < 5% of the time" → reject the null.
Small n → wide CI → everything is "maybe." Power comes from sample size.
A non-significant result ≠ proof of nothing; it means "not enough evidence".

title: A/B testing — the only clean causation machine
text: Correlation watches; experiment does. Split users randomly, change exactly one thing, and the difference in outcomes is the effect — confounders have no time to sneak in. Slide the true lift (what the new design really does) and the sample size, then play. Watch how tiny effects need huge n to become "significant" — and how a 0-lift still produces fake winners ~5% of the time. Random split = the engine that kills confounders. Change ONE variable at a time. Significant = the observed gap would be this big by luck alone < 5% of the time. Power: small lift + small n → mostly "no verdict." Bigger n is the only honest fix. Peeking daily and stopping at the first "significant" inflates false wins (the peeking problem).

title: Python for data
text: The tool of the trade: variables, structures, pandas, and the EDA pipeline

title: Variables, types & flow — the recipe of a program
text:
A program is a recipe the machine follows in order. A variable is a labelled jar: put a value in, read it out, overwrite it — the label always points at the newest value.
Trace the four lines below. The watch box on the right shows every jar after each line. Note line 3: "sum: " + str(y) — a sentence made by gluing text and a number (Python won't glue them unless you convert).
Names point at values; x = 5 then x = 7 means x is 7 — the 5 is gone.
Types matter: 5 + "5" is an error in Python; "5" * 3 is "555".
str(), int(), float() convert between types — data work is 50% conversions.
Flow is top-to-bottom; if is the only place the recipe forks.

title: Lists, dicts & sets — three ways to group things
text:
A list is an ordered shelf (positions matter). A dict is a phonebook (key → value, order irrelevant). A set is a guest list with no repeats (membership only).
Left: a list — click a position to insert 40, click the end to pop. Right: a dict — click a key to fetch its value in one hash. Notice the dict never cares about order; the list never cares about keys. Picking the wrong container is the most common beginner slowness.
List [..]: ordered, indexable, duplicates OK. append O(1); inserting at position 0 is O(n).
Dict {k: v}: key→value, lookup O(1) average (a hash table under the hood).
Set {..}: unique values, "in" check O(1) — the dedup tool of choice.
If you find yourself looping to look for something, you probably need a dict/set instead of a list.

title: Loops & comprehensions — do it to every item
text:
Data work is 90% "do this to each row." A loop is the machine's version of "take the next one from the pile." A comprehension is the same idea in one line — the idiom you'll see everywhere.
Left: the classic for-loop, stepped tile by tile. Right: the same work as squares = [x*x for x in nums] — read it right-to-left: "for each x in nums, keep x*x." If you can say a comprehension out loud in English, you own it.
for x in coll: — Python hands you each item; avoid tracking indexes by hand.
Comprehension: [expr for x in coll if cond] = map + filter in one line.
range(n) gives 0…n−1 — the classic off-by-one source: it stops BEFORE n.
Loops transform item by item — the output list grows one item per pass.

title: Functions — named machines with input, body, output
text:
A function is a vending machine: hand it an input (coin), it runs a fixed process, hands back an output. The caller never sees (or cares about) the mechanism.
Step through square(4): the call creates a frame (a private workspace with its own x), the body computes, and return hands the value back to the caller. Two calls with different inputs reuse the same body — that's the whole point.
def name(params): defines once; name(args) calls any number of times.
Each call gets a FRESH frame — its variables don't leak out (local scope).
return ends the call and hands back exactly one value.
No return = None — a function that only prints or mutates returns nothing.

title: pandas DataFrames — the spreadsheet that obeys
text:
pandas is a table in memory with a brain: select columns, filter rows, group, fill gaps — each operation returns a new table you can chain. This is 80% of day-to-day analyst code.
A dirty 6-row frame below (one missing amount, one duplicate, two small rows). Play the 4 cleaning steps and watch the frame shrink and transform. The chain df.dropna().drop_duplicates()… reads left-to-right like a sentence.
A DataFrame = columns of one type + an index. Think "typed table."
df[col] selects, df[cond] filters, df.groupby(col).agg() summarizes.
.dropna() / .fillna() / .drop_duplicates() are the three dirty-data basics.
Operations return NEW frames — the original is untouched until you assign (chain-friendly).

title: NumPy & vectorization — one op on a million items
text:
Python loops are slow because every step is a full interpreter round-trip. NumPy pushes the whole operation into optimized C running on the array at once — "vectorization" is why data science lives on NumPy/pandas.
Race below: the left lane does for i: out[i] = xs[i] * 2 (one brick per tick). The right lane does xs * 2 (the whole belt at once). Both end with the same output; watch the counters.
import numpy as np; xs = np.array([…]) = a typed, contiguous array.
xs * 2 multiplies EVERY element — no loop visible, C code underneath.
Typical speedup 50–1000× on real-sized data; that's the entire pitch.
pandas is built on NumPy — df.col * 2 gets the same win on tables.

title: EDA: load → clean → explore → visualize → question
text:
Exploratory Data Analysis is the fixed ritual before any modeling: get it in, fix what's broken, look at everything, then let the data ask you questions you didn't think to ask.
Chips = records. Two are dirty (one missing value, one duplicate). Play the pipeline and watch the dirty chips get flagged at the cleaning station, and the visualize station turn the survivors into a chart. The last station is the payoff: a question the data raised.
EDA output is QUESTIONS, not answers — "why is Lyon's amount 3× Paris's?" is a great EDA result.
The 4 classics to check: missing values, duplicates, outliers, type mix-ups.
Plot EVERY numeric column (histograms) — the first pass catches 80% of the surprises.
EDA is iterative: each question sends you back for a second look.

title: Machine learning
text: From hand-written rules to models that learn: fitting, gradients, overfitting, and the deep-learning stack

title: What is ML? Learn the rule from examples, don't write it
text:
Classic code: you write the rules, the computer follows them. ML: you show labeled examples, the machine finds a general rule that explains them — and applies it to things it has never seen.
Same task two ways. Approach A (rules) works until every edge case needs its own line. Approach B (learning) keeps one model and improves it when it gets something wrong — that loop is all of machine learning.
A model is a function f(x) → prediction whose INSIDE gets tuned automatically, not hand-written.
Labels (the answers) are the teacher; unlabeled data is the raw material.
Generalization = performing well on NEW data — the only metric that counts.
Every ML project is the same loop: predict → measure error → adjust → repeat.

title: Train / validation / test — never peek at the exam
text:
A model graded on the data it studied from looks brilliant. Graded on data it never saw, reality speaks. The split exists to keep those two numbers honest and separate.
20 labeled rows below. Step through: the TRAIN stack teaches, the VALIDATION stack helps you tune choices (learning rate, depth), and the TEST stack is graded exactly once for the final report. If the test ever influences a decision, its number is worthless.
Typical split: ~70–80% train, ~10–15% validation, ~10–15% test — all random, all disjoint.
Tuning on the test = data leakage: you've (indirectly) fitted to it; the reported number inflates.
Train ≫ val accuracy? The model memorized (overfit). Both low? It underfits.
The test set is evidence about the future; spending it on experiments burns the evidence.

title: Linear regression — click to build, and the line chases least error
text:
The simplest model: a straight line y = m·x + b. It's chosen by minimizing the Sum of Squared Errors (SSE) — the total squared distance from every point to the line. Every fancy model later is a generalization of this idea.
The line below is the least-squares fit through the 8 dots (slope and intercept are solved in closed form). CLICK the plot to add up to 12 points — the line re-fits live, residual dashes show each point's error, and SSE updates on the right.
SSE = Σ(yᵢ − ŷᵢ)². Squaring makes errors positive, punishes big misses hard, and keeps the math smooth (differentiable).
For a single line there's a formula (normal equations) — but most real models have no formula, hence gradient descent (next step).
Correlation ≠ fit: a line fits the TREND; points can still be far from it (residuals).
Always plot residuals after fitting — if they show a curve, a line was the wrong shape.

title: Gradient descent — walk downhill, one baby step at a time
text:
Most models have no closed-form solution, so the machine iterates: compute the slope of the error at the current point (the gradient), take a step opposite it. Step size = learning rate × slope. That's it — everything else is engineering around this loop.
The curve is a loss bowl; the ball sits at the current model. Press Play to step. Drag the LEARNING RATE: small = slow crawl, medium = clean descent, large = oscillation and divergence (the ball escapes and gets reset).
Step: w ← w − lr · ∂loss/∂w. The gradient is 'the slope of the error' — pointing uphill, so we go opposite.
Learning rate is THE hyperparameter: too small = glacially slow, too large = oscillates or diverges.
Near the bottom the slope → 0, so steps shrink automatically — the ball settles.
This same loop trains a line, a tree-ensemble, and a 100-billion-parameter LLM. Same math, bigger scale.

title: SGD, momentum & Adam — downhill with personality
text:
Raw gradient descent is brittle: noisy slopes stall it, narrow ravines make it zigzag. Momentum adds inertia (a shopping cart keeps rolling), Adam scales each step by the recent step-history (self-adjusting stride). Race them on the same bumpy curve.
Three identical noisy loss curves. All three particles start at the same point on the left and use the same raw slope information — only the step rule differs. Watch who settles at the bottom first and who gets trapped bouncing in the noise.
SGD: w ← w − lr·g. Simple, but noise makes it jitter and stall on plateaus.
Momentum: v ← βv − lr·g; w ← w + v. Inertia cancels consistent noise and accelerates through flat stretches.
Adam: momentum + per-parameter stride scaling — robust to noisy gradients; the default for deep learning.
These are 'first-order' methods — they only use the slope. The math is trivial; the behavior is profound.

title: Overfitting — when the model memorizes the noise
text:
More capacity fits the training data better. Past a sweet spot it stops learning the pattern and starts memorizing the noise — training error keeps falling, test error starts rising. The U-curve on the right is the single most important picture in ML.
The blue dots are the training data (a sine wave + noise); the yellow diamonds are HELD-OUT test points the model never trained on. Drag the POLYNOMIAL DEGREE: 1 underfits (a line can't bend), 2–3 tracks the wave, 7–8 threads the noise — watch it whip through every training dot while the test points are ignored.
Underfit (bias): model too simple — both errors high.
Overfit (variance): model too flexible — train error → 0, test error rises.
The sweet spot is where VALIDATION error is minimum — that's how you pick complexity in practice.
Regularization (L1/L2) is a dial that nudges the sweet spot toward simpler models.

title: K-nearest neighbours — classify by the local crowd
text:
The simplest model that isn't a line: to label a new point, look at the K closest labelled points and let the majority vote. There is no training phase at all — the model IS the data.
Two labelled crowds (blue = class A, yellow = class B). The white probe is yours: CLICK anywhere to move it. The K nearest points get connected, their classes are tallied, and the faint background shows the whole decision boundary. Drag K: small = jagged boundary that chases noise, large = smooth but blunt.
KNN has no training: prediction = find K nearest, majority vote. Simple, interpretable, and a baseline that always works.
K is a hyperparameter: small K → wiggly, noise-sensitive boundary; large K → smooth, but ignores local structure.
Distance metric matters (Euclidean is the default); features must be scaled the same way or big-scale features dominate.
Cost at prediction time grows with the data (a sca

title: Decision trees — a flowchart of yes/no questions
text:
The model is a flowchart: each internal node asks one question ("amount > 50?"), each branch answers yes or no, each leaf is a prediction. Questions are chosen to purify the split — Gini impurity is the standard yardstick.
12 loan applications (amount, age, approved?). The tree grows in three steps. Step 1 splits on amount > 50: the right side is PURE (all approved) → leaf "YES". Step 2 refines the left side with age < 30: one more pure leaf, and one imperfect leaf (2 of 3 approved — the majority wins). Gini 0 = pure; Gini 0.5 = maximally mixed.
Gini = 2·p·(1−p). A pure node (all one class) has Gini 0; a 50/50 mix has Gini 0.5. Splits maximize the Gini DROP.
Trees are interpretable: every prediction is a chain of human-readable questions — rare in ML.
A single tree overfits (it can grow until every leaf is pure); depth limits and pruning control that.
Trees hate one feature dominating: s

title: Logistic regression — squeeze a line into a probability
text:
Linear regression predicts numbers; classification needs a decision. Logistic regression runs a line's output through the sigmoid, squashing it into 0…1 — a probability — and you choose where to draw the decision threshold.
Left: the sigmoid and the current threshold. Right: two classes and the decision line at p = threshold. Drag the THRESHOLD: it moves the line, and the trade-off between 'miss a class-1' and 'falsely call class-1' shifts. Note the name: it's REGRESSION (fits a line) whose output is a PROBABILITY.
p = sigmoid(w·x + b). The sigmoid squashes any real number into (0, 1) — a probability.
The threshold converts probability → decision. Lower it = call more positives (more recall, more false alarms).
Output is calibrated: p = 0.8 means '80% of points like this were class 1 in the training data.'
Coefficients stay interpretable: wᵢ is how much feature i pushes the log-odds up o

title: K-means — clustering without any labels
text:
No labels, no teacher — just points and a number K. K-means alternates two moves: (1) every point joins its nearest centroid, (2) each centroid moves to the middle of its members. Repeat until nothing moves. The groups discover themselves.
36 unlabeled points that secretly form 3 blobs. Press Play: the three centroids (stars) start at the corners and iterate — colors show each point's current team, and the stars glide to their team's center. Drag K to 2 or 4 and re-run: the data votes on what K it really is.
Input: points + K. That's it — no labels, no features to predict. Output: K groups + centroids.
Each iteration strictly lowers the total within-cluster distance, so it always converges — but possibly to a local minimum (restart with random seeds).
K is a decision: the 'elbow' of the within-cluster-distance curve, or the silhouette score, guides the choice.

title: PCA — rotate the axes to where the data actually spreads
text:
Correlated columns carry the same information twice. Principal Component Analysis rotates the axes so the FIRST axis points along the maximum spread (variance). Most real data is 'long and thin' — so one new axis can hold most of the information, and dimensions can be thrown away.
The cloud below is deliberately elongated at 35°. The arrows are the principal components: PC1 (gold) runs along the spread, PC2 (purple) perpendicular. Switch to 'keep 1 dim' and every point is projected onto PC1 — watch the loss: only ~7% of the information (the thin sideways jitter) is discarded.
PC1 = direction of MAXIMUM variance; PC2 = max variance left after PC1, always perpendicular.
'Variance captured' tells you what 93% means: the projected data explains 93% of total spread.
Dimensionality reduction = keep the top k components, drop the rest — cheaper storage + faster models + less noise.

title: Cross-validation — rotate the exam across k folds
text:
One train/test split wastes most data for training and gets lucky-or-unlucky by which rows happened to land in the test set. K-fold cross-validation: cut the data into k folds, and take turns letting EACH fold be the exam. Average the k scores — a sturdier estimate that trains on more data every round.
40 rows cut into 5 folds (8 rows each). Step through: each turn, ONE fold (gold) holds out as the test set while the other four (blue) train the model. After five rounds every row has been an exam question exactly once, and you hold five scores to average.
k is usually 5 or 10 — a bias/variance trade-off between the estimate and the compute cost.
Every row is training data k−1 times and test data once — no row is wasted, no row is over-graded.
Use CV on the TRAIN+VAL data; the reserved TEST split still grades the final model once.
'5-fold CV, 81.2% ± 1.4%' is the honest way to report a mod

title: The confusion matrix — accuracy is not enough
text:
On 95% of a 'rare disease' dataset, the model that always says 'healthy' scores 95% and is worthless. The confusion matrix exposes this: it separates the four outcomes — true positives, false positives, false negatives, true negatives — and from them come precision, recall, and F1.
A smoke detector on 10 days: some days there's a real fire (F), some not (N); the alarm either sounds (A) or stays silent (–). Step through the 10 outcomes and watch the matrix cells count up. Precision = 'of the alarms, how many were real'; Recall = 'of the real fires, how many we caught'.
TP = caught it right · FP = false alarm · FN = missed it · TN = correctly quiet.
Precision = TP/(TP+FP): trust in a positive call. Recall = TP/(TP+FN): coverage of the positives.
F1 = harmonic mean of precision & recall — one number when you need to balance both.
Pick the metric from the COST matrix: spam → precision first;

title: ROC & AUC — one curve for every possible threshold
text:
A good classifier emits PROBABILITIES; the threshold is a policy choice. The ROC curve plots TPR (you caught the real ones) against FPR (you falsely accused the innocent) while sweeping the threshold from strict to loose. The area under that curve (AUC) is the model's skill, threshold-free.
Left: 40 fire scores (gold) and 40 no-fire scores (blue) — they overlap. The threshold line decides who 'alarms'. Right: the ROC curve — the point rides it as you drag the threshold. A perfect model hugs the top-left corner (AUC 1.0); a coin flip draws the diagonal (AUC 0.5).
TPR = TP/(TP+FN) — you caught the fires. FPR = FP/(FP+TN) — false alarms per innocent.
Sweep the threshold: every threshold is one (FPR, TPR) point; connect them → the ROC curve.
AUC = 'if I pick one random fire and one random no-fire, the model ranks the fire higher.' AUC 0.8 = 80% of the time.
Calibration matters separately: AU

title: Ensembles — the committee beats the genius
text:
One strong model is good; a committee of many slightly-wrong models that disagree is better. Random forest = many decision trees on shuffled data, majority vote. Gradient boosting = each new model fixes the previous model's mistakes. The math: if errors are independent, averaging cancels the noise and keeps the signal.
The target is circular (inner disk = class 1, outer ring = class 0) — no single line separates it well. Left: 15 'weak' lines, each ~60–75% accurate alone. Right: the majority vote of all 15 — watch the jagged individual errors average out into a near-circular boundary. This is the random-forest intuition in its purest form.
Bagging (random forest): many models on shuffled subsets, independent, average the votes → variance drops.
Boosting: models train SEQUENTIALLY on the previous model's mistakes → bias drops (XGBoost, LightGBM).
Both need DIVERSE members: identical model

title: Neural networks — stacked weighted sums that can draw curves
text:
One neuron computes a weighted sum plus a non-linearity (a sigmoid squish). Stack layers of them and the composition can approximate ANY boundary — circles, spirals, faces. The network has no special knowledge of 'circles'; that shape EMERGES from the stacked sums.
A 2→4→4→1 network. Press Play to run the forward pass: the input (price high = 0.8, rating low = 0.3) flows right, each neuron sums its inputs with its weights and squishes through a sigmoid, and the single output neuron says 'churn probability 0.83'. The hot edges show where the signal is at each step.
Neuron: z = Σ wᵢxᵢ + b, then a = sigmoid(z). That's the ENTIRE unit — everything else is repetition.
Without the non-linearity, stacking layers collapses to one big linear layer — the squish is what lets layers bend the boundary.
Width = how many different 'feature detectors' per layer; depth = how many refinement passes.
Train

title: Backpropagation — send the blame backwards
text:
Forward pass: predict. Compare with the truth: error. Backward pass: each weight gets a share of the blame — the derivative of the loss with respect to that weight — and nudges against it. This blame-distribution algorithm is backprop, and it is how every modern model learns.
A tiny 2→2→1 network, one training example (truth = 0, prediction = 0.86). Step through: forward → error → blame flows back along the edges (red, sized by blame) → weights nudge against their blame → re-run: prediction 0.54. Repeat a few thousand times and the error is ~0. The sparkline is that repetition.
Backprop = the chain rule, automated: ∂loss/∂w for every weight, computed right-to-left in one sweep.
Blame is PROPORTIONAL: a weight on a hot path (large incoming signal) takes more blame than one on a cold one.
The update is identical to gradient descent: w ← w − lr·blame. No new math, just efficient bookkeeping

title: Convolutions — a small filter, slid over the whole image
text:
A CNN's first layer slides a tiny filter (e.g. 3×3) over every position of the image, computing one number per position: 'how much of this pattern is here?' One filter = one feature detector. The output is a new, smaller 'feature map' image where that pattern glows.
The image (left) is a dark band above a bright band — one horizontal edge. The filter (center, moving) is an edge detector: −1 on the top row, +1 on the bottom row. Press Play: it slides left-to-right, top-to-bottom, and stamps its response into the feature map (right). Only the rows where dark MEETS bright light up.
One filter = one pattern; a layer stacks many filters (edges in all directions, textures, colors).
The SAME weights are used at every position — 'weight sharing'. Fewer parameters, and the detector works no matter where the pattern is.
Stacking layers composes features: edges → corners → textures → shapes → objec

title: Recurrent networks — the same block, run over time
text:
Sequences need memory. An RNN runs ONE block repeatedly: at each time step it reads the new token, updates a hidden state h (a running summary of everything so far), and moves on. The loop IS the architecture — one set of weights, shared across every step.
The sentence '… it was tired' arrives word by word. At each step the block updates the hidden state (the three bars on the right — a 3-dim summary). Watch the moment 'it' arrives: the network must know 'it' = CAT, and 'cat' left the input window 6 steps ago — only the hidden state carries that link forward.
hₜ = tanh(W·xₜ + U·hₜ₋₁): the new state mixes the new token with the old state. One formula, every step.
The hidden state is the model's working memory — and in a plain RNN it fades (the vanishing gradient problem).
Long-range links ("it" → "cat") are hard: the signal must survive many steps of blending.
Gates (LSTM) and attention (

title: Attention — let every word look at every word
text:
RNNs compress the past into one fading vector; attention deletes the bottleneck. Every token directly LOOKS at every other token and assigns a weight: 'how much should I copy from you?' Long-range links ('it' → 'cat') are now ONE lookup, no matter the distance.
Eight tokens, one sentence. The matrix shows every token's attention to every other (row = who's looking, column = who's looked at). Click a token: its row highlights, and arcs show where it actually 'looks' — note how 'it' mostly looks at 'cat' and 'tired', not at its immediate neighbours.
Attention weight = softmax(Q·Kᵀ/√d): each token's query against every other token's key, normalized to sum to 1.
'Self'-attention: queries and keys come from the SAME sequence — every token updates itself from the whole context.
Distance no longer costs: 'it'→'cat' is one lookup whether the gap is 6 words or 6000 — this is what made long docume

title: LLMs & RAG — the model is the brain, your data is the notebook
text:
A large language model predicts the next token from its context window — brilliant, but it knows NOTHING about your company unless you tell it. RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) closes the gap: embed your documents, search for the ones relevant to the question, paste the top snippets INTO the prompt, and the model answers grounded in your data.
Step through the RAG pipeline for the question 'What's the EU refund window?': the question is embedded and matched against document embeddings (similar meaning = nearby dots); the top-2 snippets are stuffed into the prompt window; the model generates an answer that CITES the snippet. Without RAG, the same model would guess from memory — plausible-sounding, possibly wrong.
An LLM = next-token prediction at enormous scale; it has no memory between chats and no knowledge of your files.
Embeddings put similar MEANINGS near each other in a vector s

title: Data structures & algorithms
text: How to store and find things fast: complexity, arrays, trees, graphs, sorting, searching

title: Big-O — counting steps, not seconds
text:
Before any code, the analyst's question: how does the work grow as the data grows? Big-O names the growth shape: O(1) constant, O(log n) halving, O(n) linear, O(n²) quadratic. Two programs that tie at n = 1,000 can differ by YEARS at n = 100,000,000.
Drag N and watch the four lanes. The bar is the operation count on a LOG scale (each screen width = ×1000); the chip is real time assuming a fast machine at 1,000,000,000 ops/sec. n² is the lane that destroys careers.
Big-O keeps only the dominant term: 3n² + 40n = O(n²). Constants and small terms are noise at scale.
O(log n) = 'halve the search space each step' — binary search, balanced trees.
Rule of thumb: O(n) at 10⁸ ≈ a tenth of a second; O(n²) at 10⁸ ≈ months. Structure choice IS the performance.
Data analysts meet this constantly: nested loops over two big tables are the n² in your pipeline.

title: Arrays — random access is free, insertion is a relay race
text:
An array is one contiguous block of memory. Because every cell is the same size, the machine computes the address of position i in one arithmetic step — that's why reading a[i] is O(1). But everything is glued together: insert at the front and every element must shift.
Five-element array below. Step 2: read a[3] — one hop, no scan. Step 3: insert 99 at position 0 — watch the relay: 4 elements move. Insertions at the END are cheap (O(1)); at the FRONT they're O(n). That asymmetry shapes how you build pipelines (append-heavy, not prepend-heavy).
a[i] = base_address + i·cell_size — one computation, O(1) read.
Append at end: O(1) amortized (occasional resize). Insert at 0: O(n) shifts.
Fixed size (in C) vs dynamic (Python list grows for you) — same address math underneath.
If you're inserting at the front in a loop, you've accidentally built O(n²) — switch to a deque or prepend a marker.

title: Stack vs queue — two ways to hold a line
text:
Both hold items in order; they differ on WHERE you add and remove. Stack: add and remove at the TOP (last in, first out — a pile of plates). Queue: add at the back, remove at the FRONT (first in, first out — a waiting line).
Both structures receive A, B, C in the same order. Then the stack POPS and the queue DEQUEUES — watch which item leaves. This one flip (LIFO vs FIFO) is behind undo buttons (stack), function calls (stack), printer jobs (queue), and task queues (queue).
Stack (LIFO): push/pop at top, both O(1). Undo history, browser back, call stack, DFS.
Queue (FIFO): enqueue back, dequeue front, both O(1). Printer jobs, BFS, rate limiters, message systems (Kafka-style).
Peek = look without removing — free on both.
A deque does both ends; Python's collections.deque and JS (push/shift — beware, shift is O(n) on plain arrays).

title: Linked lists — cells that point to their neighbour
text:
A linked list stores items in separate boxes scattered in memory; each box holds a POINTER to the next. No contiguous block, no address math — you reach anything by WALKING from the head, one pointer at a time.
4-node list below. Walking to node 3 costs 3 pointer hops (O(k)). But inserting a new node after node 1 is TWO pointer rewrites — zero element movement. Arrays buy fast reads and pay for inserts; lists buy fast inserts and pay for reads. They are opposites.
Each node: [value | next]. The head is the only address you keep.
Read the k-th node: O(k) hops. Arrays did that in O(1).
Insert after a known node: O(1) pointer surgery (two rewires). Arrays did that in O(n).
A doubly-linked list adds a prev pointer — remove any node in O(1) once you have it.

title: Hash tables — the O(1) look-up machine
text:
A hash table maps keys to buckets: bucket = hash(key) % size. The hash function scatters similar-looking keys across the table, so a lookup is: compute the bucket, walk the (short) chain there. Average cost: constant, no matter how many keys exist.
Six buckets. Step through: Ana hashes to bucket 2, Ben to 1, Cara to 2 — a COLLISION, so Cara hangs on Ana's chain. Lookup of 'Cara': one hash, then check 2 names. Collisions are expected — the table is sized so chains stay short, which is what keeps the average at O(1).
hash(key) is a deterministic function: same key → same bucket, every time.
Collisions are normal; resolved by chaining (list per bucket) or open addressing.
Load factor = keys/buckets; rehash (resize + re-insert all) keeps it < ~0.7 → O(1) average.
This is the engine under Python dict, JS object, SQL's join optimization, and your 'is this email a duplicate?' check.

title: Binary search trees — sorted structure, log-depth search
text:
A BST stores sorted data in a tree: left child < node < right child. That one rule means every comparison ELIMINATES HALF the remaining candidates — search, insert, delete all run in O(log n) on a balanced tree. Same rule on sorted input = a degenerate line (O(n)).
Insert 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 80 — each new value compares down from the root until it finds its gap. Then the final step searches for 40: 50 → 30 → 40, three hops. The panel on the right shows what happens when you insert already-sorted data: the 'tree' collapses into a line and every operation costs O(n).
Invariant: left < node < right. Search: at each node, half the candidates are gone.
Balanced tree: depth ≈ log₂(n). 1,000,000 nodes → depth ≈ 20.
Sorted inserts destroy balance → depth n → O(n) everywhere. AVL/red-black trees re-balance automatically.
In-order traversal (left, node, right) outputs the keys in sorted order — fr

title: Graphs — BFS rings vs DFS dives
text:
A graph is nodes + edges — the general shape of 'things connected to things.' Two canonical walks: BFS explores in RINGS (nearest neighbours first — shortest paths, Facebook 'degrees of separation'), DFS dives to a LEAF before backtracking (puzzles, cycle detection, topological order).
Seven nodes, seven edges. Toggle BFS / DFS and play: BFS lights up level by level (A → {B,C} → {D,E,F} → G); DFS walks A→B→D→G, backtracks, then E, then C→F. Same graph, completely different visit orders — pick the walk for the question you're asking.
BFS (queue): visits in distance order → finds the SHORTEST unweighted path.
DFS (stack/recursion): goes deep, backtracks → cycle detection, topological sort, 'is it reachable at all?'.
Both visit every node exactly once; both are O(V + E).
Analyst context: ad-click funnels, dependency graphs, fraud rings — all of it is graph walking.

title: Sorting — bubble the simple, conquer the smart
text:
Sorting is the algorithmic workhorse: 90% of 'find the top/bottom/median' questions are one sort away. Bubble sort is O(n²) — simple, and the reason for its infamy. Quicksort is O(n log n) average — partition around a pivot, recurse on the halves. At n = 1,000,000 the difference is minutes vs milliseconds.
Same 7-element array, two engines. Play BUBBLE: neighbour comparisons and swaps, pass by pass. Play QUICKSORT: pivot selection, partition swaps, recursion. The step counters make the n log n vs n² gap concrete — and explain why every library sort (Timsort in Python, introsort in C++) is a divide-and-conquer hybrid, never bubble.
Bubble: adjacent compare-swap, n passes — O(n²). Educational only.
Quicksort: pick pivot, partition (smaller left, bigger right), recurse — O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst on sorted input with bad pivots.
Python's built-in sort is TIMSORT: mergesort + insertion

title: Searching — linear scan vs binary halving
text:
Unsorted data: scan it (O(n)) — no shortcut exists. Sorted data: halve the search range every step (O(log n)). One value, two orders of magnitude apart at scale: 10⁸ items take 10⁸ checks linearly, or 27 checks binary.
Ten sorted values, target = 82 (near the end — the worst case for a lucky scan). Play LINEAR: check 0, 1, 2, … until 82. Play BINARY: jump to the middle, keep the half that can contain 82, repeat. The window shading shows the alive half of the array.
Linear search: O(n), works on ANY data (sorted or not).
Binary search: O(log n), REQUIRES sorted order (or a sorted index).
27 binary checks cover 10⁸ items; a linear scan takes 10⁸.
SQL 'WHERE x = 5' on a non-indexed column is a linear scan; on an indexed column it's a B-tree lookup (binary-search family).

title: Data engineering
text: Moving, storing, and preparing data at scale: clusters, distributed logs, warehouses, and the pipelines that feed them

title: Scale — the moment one machine stops being enough
text:
Every data system hits the same wall: data grows, but one machine's disk, CPU, and memory do not. Two escapes: scale UP (bigger machine — linear money, hard physical ceiling) or scale OUT (many machines sharing the load — the entire field of data engineering).
Drag the day's data volume. Both panels process the same data: the gauge shows how loaded each machine is (against a 24h daily SLA), the bars show how long the batch takes. Single machine: one bar, one ceiling. Cluster of 3: the work splits, each bar is a third. Watch where red starts.
Scale out = parallelism: work that is independent per row/file/customer divides across machines almost for free.
Scale up = one bigger box: cost grows linearly (and hardware grows super-linearly), and you hit a physical ceiling: one disk, one RAM, one failure.
HDFS, Spark, Kafka all exist to make scale-out routine: chunk it, spread it, aggregate it.

title: HDFS — big files, chopped into blocks, copied 3×
text:
One 768GB file can't live on one disk, and one dead disk must not lose the data. HDFS's answer: split the file into 128MB blocks, scatter the blocks across many machines, and keep THREE copies of every block on different nodes. A node dying is an event, not an incident.
Step through: the file is split, a NameNode keeps the MAP (block → which nodes), and each block is replicated to three DataNodes. Then node B dies — its blocks are still served from their two surviving replicas, and the NameNode schedules fresh copies. Nothing is lost, nothing stops.
NameNode = metadata only: 'block 7 lives on nodes A, B, C'. It never touches the bytes.
DataNodes = the bytes: each block stored on 3 different nodes (in production: 3 different racks).
128MB block size: big enough to make reads efficient, small enough to spread load and survive failures.
Client reads a block from the NEAREST replica — parall

title: MapReduce — split the work, shuffle the keys, reduce the totals
text:
MapReduce is the pattern the whole field was built on: MAP each input row independently (emit key/value pairs), SHUFFLE (sort+group all pairs by key — the expensive, network-heavy heart), REDUCE (aggregate each key's group). Any computation that is 'sum per group' fits this shape.
Six sales rows. Play the three phases: each row MAPS to a (city, amount) pair; the SHUFFLE groups pairs by city; each REDUCER sums its group. The output is one table: revenue per city. Same pattern, ten million rows and ten thousand reducers — that's the job.
MAP is embarrassingly parallel — each row is independent, any machine can do it.
SHUFFLE = the network bottleneck: all pairs with the same key must land on the same reducer (partitioned by hash of key).
REDUCE receives ONE key at a time, already sorted — aggregation is trivial.
This exact shape (emit → group-by → aggregate) is what SQL's GROUP BY, Spark's

title: Spark — a DAG that keeps intermediates in memory
text:
MapReduce writes EVERY stage's output to disk before the next stage can start. Spark builds the whole job as a DAG of stages and keeps the shuffle data in RAM between them — so a 4-stage job pays the disk tax once instead of three times. For iterative work (machine learning!), the difference is 10–100×.
The same 4-stage job (read → filter → join → aggregate) two ways. Top: MapReduce — every arrow passes through a DISK (write + read back). Bottom: Spark — arrows pass through RAM. Then the timing bars: 3 disk round-trips vs none. The last step shows why ML teams live in Spark: 50 passes over the same data.
A 'stage' = work between shuffles. The shuffle boundary is where data changes machines — and in MapReduce, where it hits disk.
Spark's shuffle is in-memory (with disk spill as overflow) — the stage boundary costs milliseconds, not minutes.
Iterative algorithms (gradient descent, k-means)

title: Kafka — an append-only log, partitioned by design
text:
Kafka's core is not a 'queue' — it's a COMMITTED LOG: messages are appended, never modified, each with an offset. A topic is split into PARTITIONS (independent ordered logs), and messages with the same key always hash to the same partition — which is how you get ordering guarantees at scale.
Six steps: the log concept, key-based partitioning, appends, consumers with offsets, a burst that creates LAG, and catch-up. Note what never happens: messages are never reordered inside a partition, and a slow consumer's lag is visible as a number — you can watch it grow and shrink.
Append-only + offsets = replay: any consumer can re-read from any offset within the retention window.
Key-based hashing → same key, same partition → per-partition ordering (global ordering is impossible by design).
Consumer GROUP: each partition is consumed by exactly one member — scale consumers to add throughput, not to

title: Lake vs warehouse — schema-on-read vs schema-on-write
text:
A data LAKE stores files as-is: cheap, flexible, but the schema is only applied when you query (and you pay that cost every query). A data WAREHOUSE validates and structures data AT WRITE time (star schema, types, keys) so queries run on pre-shaped, pre-indexed tables. Modern shops run both: lake for raw flexibility, warehouse for the reporting layer.
Left: the lake. Files land as-is; a query must parse, apply a schema, and scan every row — every single time. Right: the warehouse. Ingest validates and loads into a star schema (one fact table, satellite dimensions); a query is an index lookup. Same data, opposite costs — and the costs happen on opposite sides of the pipeline.
Schema-on-read (lake): flexibility + cheap storage; you pay schema work at query time, and mistakes surface late.
Schema-on-write (warehouse): validation at ingest; queries are fast and consistent, but new data shape

title: The OLAP cube — slice, dice, roll up
text:
Every business question is a cell in a cube: dimensions (TIME, REGION, PRODUCT…) are the axes, and the MEASURE (sales) is the value in each cell. OLAP operations are just ways of grouping the cube: SLICE (fix one dimension to a value), DICE (fix several — one cell), ROLL UP (coarsen an axis: month → quarter), DRILL DOWN (the reverse).
Spin the cube: three axes (TIME, REGION, PRODUCT) and the measure (SALES) living in every cell. Step through the operations and watch which faces light up and what SQL each one compiles to — it's always just a GROUP BY / WHERE on the fact table.
Cell = one combination of dimension values; its value = the measure (SUM, COUNT, AVG…).
SLICE: WHERE time='Q4' — one face. DICE: WHERE time='Q4' AND region='East' — one cell (or a sub-cube).
ROLL UP: GROUP BY quarter instead of month — 12 cells collapse to 4, values pre-aggregated.
Under the hood there is no magic:

title: DAX — the formula stays still, the context moves
text:
In DAX (Power BI's formula language) a MEASURE is a formula like SUM(Sales). The formula never changes — what changes is the FILTER CONTEXT: the set of rows the formula is evaluated over. A dashboard filtered to Region=East doesn't run a different formula; it runs the SAME formula over a different slice of the table.
Six rows, one formula. Step 1: the page filter Region=East lands — the same SUM now sees 400. Step 2: add Product=Laptop — contexts INTERSECT, the result narrows to 150. Step 3: the same formula on three cards — three contexts, three answers, zero formula changes.
Measure = formula. Filter context = the rows it runs over. Result = f(formula, context).
Contexts intersect (AND): page filter + card filter + slicer all stack on the same table.
CALCULATE() is the tool that deliberately CHANGES the context inside a measure (add/remove filters).
This is why one Power BI measure ser

title: ETL — extract, transform, load (and survive the re-run)
text:
ETL is the daily plumbing: EXTRACT raw rows from sources (CRM, web logs, invoices), TRANSFORM them into one clean shape (fill nulls, parse currencies, drop duplicates), LOAD them into the warehouse. The unglamorous requirement that separates junior from senior pipelines: a re-run must be IDEMPOTENT — running the same day twice must not double the data.
Six raw rows from three sources — two are dirty (a null amount, a string currency), one is a duplicate. Play the stages: extract lands everything in staging; transform fixes what's fixable and drops the dup; load lands 5 clean rows. Step 5: the whole thing re-runs — watch the target count stay at 5.
Transform is where trust is BUILT: type coercion, null policy, dedupe keys, validation rules.
'Dirty data' is not an edge case — it's the normal state of source systems.
Idempotency: load by primary key (upsert) or truncate-and-reload the parti

title: Data quality — trust is a measured thing
text:
A dashboard is only as true as the data behind it. Quality gates make trust explicit: every batch is checked against SLAs (null rate, duplicates, value ranges, freshness) BEFORE it reaches the reporting layer. A gate that fails blocks the load and raises an alert — a dashboard showing a number that failed its checks is a lie with a nice color scheme.
A batch of 100 rows flows through four checkers into the gate. Step 1: 3 nulls appear (3% > 1% SLA) → gate goes red, dashboard stays on the last TRUSTED number. Steps 2–4: duplicates, a negative price, stale data — each alone is enough to block. The point isn't perfection; it's that bad data can't reach a human decision silently.
SLAs are numbers: nulls < 1%, dupes = 0, prices > 0, freshness < 24h. 'Looks fine' is not a check.
Gate = hard rule: fail → block the load + alert. The dashboard keeps the last known-good number (labeled as such).
N

title: Data visualization & storytelling
text: The right chart for the question, honest encoding, dashboards that survive 30 seconds, and stories that end in action

title: Pick the chart by the question, not by taste
text:
Chart choice is a mapping: each question type has a visual channel that answers it fastest. Compare magnitudes → lengths (bars). Change over time → positions along a line. Parts of a whole → angles/areas (carefully). Distribution → a histogram. Relationship between two numbers → positions in 2D (scatter). Picking the wrong tool doesn't crash — it just makes the answer harder to see.
Pick a question type below the canvas. The chart grid lights up the tool(s) that answer it, and the preview shows why it works. Notice how 'compare' and 'part of whole' are the most commonly confused pair — bars for comparison, pie only when the parts actually sum to something you care about.
Compare → bars (length). Trend → line (position on time). Shape → histogram. Relationship → scatter. Part-of-whole → pie ONLY for 2–4 parts that sum to a meaningful total.
Stacked bars = comparison AND composition at onc

title: What the eye actually compares (channel ranking)
text:
Not every visual encoding is equal. Position and length are read with ±1% accuracy. Angles: only to ~±15°. Areas: ~±30%. 3D volumes: untrustworthy — perspective, occlusion and the ellipse 'lid' all lie. This is why a bar chart beats a pie chart: it uses the eye's best channel, not its worst.
Slide the difference between two quantities (2% to 40%) and watch the same question — 'which is bigger?' — answered by four encodings. The bars stay readable the whole way; the pies need ~10%; the squares need ~20%; the cylinders never fully earn your trust.
Channel ranking: position/length ≫ angle > area > volume > color for MAGNITUDE. Color is excellent for CATEGORIES (hue = identity, not size).
Pies encode magnitude as ANGLE — the second-worst 2D channel — and 6+ slices makes each angle smaller still.
3D charts add a third axis that carries no data but corrupts the two that do (decoration with sid

title: Charts that lie — the five tricks (and how to spot them)
text:
A chart can be 100% 'accurate' (every point real, every axis labeled) and still send the reader to a wrong decision. The five classics: (1) truncated y-axis — hide the zero and a 7% change looks like a takeoff; (2) dual axis — two unrelated series on two hidden scales 'correlate'; (3) 3D distortion — volume and perspective inflate the big bars; (4) cherry-picked x-range — show only the months that suit the story; (5) stacked transfer — one series grows inside the stack while the base quietly shrinks.
The same 8 months of revenue (up 7%, honestly) under five different lies. Step through and read the panel on the right: what the chart CLAIMS vs what is actually TRUE. Your job as the analyst is to be the person who notices the y-axis before the CEO does.
Truncated y-axis: a line chart with a hidden zero turns a 7% rise into a 'cliff'. Rule: zero-based for magnitudes; truncation only for sma

title: Color systems — categorical, sequential, diverging
text:
Color has exactly three jobs, and mixing them up is the most common 'technical' lie in business charts. CATEGORICAL: distinct hues for distinct things (order means nothing — hue = identity). SEQUENTIAL: light→dark of ONE hue family for ordered magnitude (light = small, dark = big). DIVERGING: two hues meeting at a neutral midpoint around a MEANINGFUL center (zero, average, target). A map of 'deviation from target' painted in a random rainbow is not colorful — it's wrong.
Pick a system, slide the number of steps, and watch three rows: (top) the palette, (middle) a data strip using it, (bottom) what a common color-blindness (deuteranopia) actually sees. Sequential and diverging survive the color-blind row — categorical only survives while it stays small (≤5 hues).
Categorical: distinctness > order. Keep ≤5 hues; beyond that the eye can't keep the mapping, and red–green pairs vanish for ~8%

title: Dashboard layout — the 30-second rule
text:
An executive gives a dashboard about 30 seconds. The eye scans in an F-pattern: top row first, left to right. So the layout encodes importance: HEADLINE KPIs on top (the answer), TREND/CONTEXT in the middle (the story), DETAIL at the bottom (the evidence, for the curious). One dashboard, one audience, one question. Six KPIs that don't answer one question is not a dashboard — it's a wall of numbers.
Six cards start in the WRONG rows. Click any card to move it to the next row (headline → trend → detail → headline…). Reach the 6/6 score: every card in the row that matches its job. Watch the '30-second score' and the hints as you go.
Top row = the ANSWER (1–3 KPIs tied to the dashboard's one question). If you can't name the question, the dashboard doesn't exist yet.
Middle row = the TREND behind the KPIs (sparklines, funnels). Bottom row = the DETAIL tables for the curious — never in the hea

title: Data storytelling — context first, callouts last
text:
The same chart tells three different stories depending on what surrounds it. Version 1: a naked line — the reader sees 'a line… so what?'. Version 2: add CONTEXT (last year, the plan) — now the reader sees 'we missed plan in September'. Version 3: add the CALLOUT ('summer promo ended') and the ACTION ('re-run the promo Oct–Nov') — now the chart ends in a decision. A chart without a next step is decoration; a story without context is a guess.
One revenue line (the September dip is real in all four versions). Step through and watch the reader's state on the right move from 'huh?' to 'do it'. The chart never changes except for what's ADDED around it — that's the whole craft.
Order of the story: CONTEXT (what should we be seeing?) → FINDING (what are we actually seeing?) → CAUSE (why?) → ACTION (what do we do, and what changes when we do?).

title: Ship it — from notebook to career
text: The analyst loop, portfolio projects, production, communicating to execs, interviews, and your capstone

title: The analyst loop — question → data → insight → action
text:
Real analysis is not a line, it's a LOOP. A business question earns a data pull; the data earns an analysis; the analysis earns an insight; the insight earns an ACTION; and the action changes behavior, which creates NEW data, which raises the NEXT question. Analysts who work in a straight line ('crunch → report → done') stop creating value at the report. The loop is what makes the job repeatable.
Walk the five nodes of the loop with a ShopFlow example. Notice the dashed arrow: ACTION feeds back into QUESTION — that's the part most junior work is missing, and the part that gets analysts promoted.
A question without a DECISION behind it ('how many users?') is trivia, not analysis. 'Should we fix the EU checkout loss?' has money attached — that's a question worth a data pull.
Each beat earns the next: don't pull data until the question has a decision; don't present an insight without an act

title: Anatomy of a portfolio project
text:
A portfolio project is an interview that happens before the interview: a business question with money attached, real (or realistically-messy) data, a method a stranger can follow, ONE insight, an action, and documentation that survives a 10-minute read by someone who doesn't know you. Ten notebook cells of clever code with no decision is not a project — it's a demo. The six stages below are the checklist a hiring manager actually scans.
Step through the six stages of one ShopFlow project. On the right, the 'portfolio-grade' checklist lights up as each stage does its job. Notice: the question stage does the most hiring work — it's the first thing a recruiter reads and the last thing a project usually defines.
QUESTION first, with a decision: 'fix the EU checkout loss or accept it' — estimable, time-boxed, money-attached. No decision → no project.

title: Notebook to production — the three gaps
text:
A notebook that runs on your laptop is not a product. Three gaps stand between it and the real job: (1) it must RUN WITHOUT YOU — a schedule, idempotent loads, no human clicks (phase 6's ETL rules); (2) it must FAIL LOUDLY — alerts on null spikes, freshness, breakage, plus auto-retry, so a dead pipeline is discovered in minutes, not at the Monday meeting; (3) it must be CONSUMED — a dashboard or an API where decisions actually happen, not a PDF in a chat channel. Close the gaps in that order and the notebook becomes infrastructure.
Step through the three gaps. At each stage the readout names 'what breaks without this' — because the gap only exists until the thing breaks once, and it WILL break once.
Gap 1 · Run without you: a scheduler (cron) + idempotent loads (phase 6) + a versioned repo. 'Works on my machine' is the first gap, and the one that costs the most sleep.
Gap 2 · Fail loudly

title: The 30-second insight — the pyramid (execs read top-down)
text:
Executives process top-down: the recommendation first, then the two or three supporting points, then (if they still care) the evidence. Presenting bottom-up — 'let me walk you through the data' — spends their patience on the evidence before they know what you're asking for. The Pyramid is the shape: RECOMMENDATION at the top (one line), SUPPORTING POINTS below it (2–3), EVIDENCE at the base (the appendix that proves it, for whoever asks). The order you SAY things is the pyramid; the order you BUILT them doesn't matter.
Four blocks are on the table in random order. Click them in the order you would SAY them in the meeting. The pyramid builds in speaking order, and the exec's patience meter scores you: the recommendation at the top is worth the most; every block that lands out of place spends patience.
Top line = the RECOMMENDATION with the number: 'double the EU budget — revenue +$40k/wk'

title: The interview loop — technical, case, take-home
text:
Data interviews run three rounds, each testing a different muscle: (1) TECHNICAL — SQL on a whiteboard (window functions, joins, aggregates) plus pandas and stats intuition; (2) CASE — an unstructured business question ('how would you measure success of a new onboarding flow?') where framing beats fluency: goal → north-star metric + guardrails → hypotheses → data plan, in that order, before any 'data' is touched; (3) TAKE-HOME — a small project judged on depth AND communication: they often grade the one-page summary more heavily than the notebook. The common failure in all three is the same: performing at the level of the question asked, instead of the level of the decision implied.
Step through the three rounds. Each panel gives the round's format and the single highest-leverage move in it. The quiz at the end is the case round's first move — the one interviewees most often skip.

title: Your capstone — the brief (and the stranger test)
text:
The last step of the course is yours. You get a brief, a dataset, and a decision — and you run the whole course against it: the question earns the data (p1), the data earns the analysis (p2, p3), the analysis earns the insight (p4 where a model is honest), the insight earns the story (p7), and the story earns the ship (p8: A/B, docs, the pyramid email). The success criterion is the STRANGER TEST: a person who knows nothing about the project can state the question, your one insight, and the decision — in 10 minutes, unaided. Pass that and you have the first real artifact of a data career.
Pick one of the three ShopFlow briefs. The roadmap shows which phase of this course each stage draws on, and the stranger-test checklist is the definition of done. There is no 'correct' brief — there is only one you'd defend in front of a hiring manager.

title: The mutable default argument
text:
def add_item(item, basket=[]):
    basket.append(item)
    return basket

a = add_item("apple")
b = add_item("pear")
print(a)
print(b)
print(a is b)
blurb: The default is built once, at definition time, and every call that omits the argument shares it.

title: Shallow copy versus deep copy
text:
import copy

original = [1, [2, 3]]
alias = original
shallow = original[:]
deep = copy.deepcopy(original)

original[1].append(4)
original.append(9)

print(alias)
print(shallow)
print(deep)
blurb: A slice copies the outer list and shares every nested object inside it.

title: Closures capture the variable, not the value
text:
funcs = []
for i in range(3):
    funcs.append(lambda: i)

print([f() for f in funcs])

fixed = []
for i in range(3):
    fixed.append(lambda i=i: i)

print([f() for f in fixed])
blurb: Every lambda made in the loop closes over the same name, so all three see its final value.

title: A generator is lazy
text:
def counter(n):
    total = 0
    for i in range(n):
        total += i
        yield total

gen = counter(4)
print(next(gen))
print(next(gen))
rest = list(gen)
print(rest)
blurb: Nothing runs until you pull. The function resumes where it left off, keeping its frame alive.

title: Recursion and the call stack
blurb: Each call gets its own frame. Watch the stack grow, then unwind as the returns come back.

title: try / except / else / finally
blurb: Four clauses, and the two that people get wrong under questioning.

title: Inheritance, super and the MRO
blurb: super() walks the instance's MRO, not the class's own parent.

title: Why join beats += in a loop
text:
parts = ["id", "name", "city"]

joined = ""
for p in parts:
    joined += p + ","

print(joined)
print(",".join(parts))
blurb: Strings are immutable, so each += allocates a new object and copies.

title: Passing a list to a function
text:
def mutate(xs, y):
    xs.append(99)
    y = y + 1
    return y

nums = [1, 2]
count = 5
result = mutate(nums, count)

print(nums)
print(count)
print(result)
blurb: The reference is passed by value: mutation is visible, rebinding is not.

title: Java is pass-by-value, always
blurb: The reference is copied. Mutating through the copy is visible to the caller; rebinding the copy is not.

title: == versus equals, and the string pool
blurb: Literals are interned into one shared object. new String() is not, and a concatenation built in a loop is not either.

title: The Integer cache, and why == lies
blurb: Boxed values from −128 to 127 come from a shared cache. Above that, every box is a new object.

title: Overriding is dynamic, static methods are not
blurb: Instance methods dispatch on the runtime type. Static methods bind at compile time to the declared type.

title: What finally does to a return
blurb: The return value is captured before finally runs. A return inside finally replaces it — and swallows exceptions.

title: try-with-resources closes in reverse
blurb: Three resources open in order and close in the opposite order, before catch and before finally.

title: X.4 Kafka, Avro, Delivery Semantics, and Schema Evolution
text: X.4 Kafka, Avro, Delivery Semantics, and Schema Evolution Kafka stores ordered records in partitions. A topic can scale across partitions, but ordering is guaranteed only within a partition. Choose a message key—such as order_id—to place related events in the same partition. Consumer groups divide partitions among consumers; a partition is processed by at most one member of a group at a time. The producer must balance durability and throughput. Important controls include acknowledgements, retries, idempotence, batching, compression, and timeouts. Consumers manage offsets, processing, and commits. text: X.7 Python MRO, __slots__, and Pandas Reshaping Python’s method resolution order (MRO) defines how attribute lookup proceeds through multiple inheritance. Python uses C3 linearization, which preserves local precedence and a consistent ordering. Cooperative classes call super() so each class in the MRO participates once. class Audited: def save(self): print("audit") return super().save() class Persisted: def save(self): print("persist") class Order(Audited, Persisted): pass print(Order.mro()) Order().save() __slots__ declares a fixed set of instance attributes and can reduce per-instance memory by avoiding a normal __dict__. # ===== psycopg2 (PostgreSQL) =====
import psycopg2
from psycopg2.extras import RealDictCursor

def get_connection():
    return psycopg2.connect(
        host="localhost",
        database="mydb",
        user="user",
        password="password"
    )

# CREATE
def create_user(name, email):
    conn = get_connection()
    try:
        with conn.cursor() as cur:
            cur.execute(
                "INSERT INTO users (name, email) VALUES (%s, %s) RETURNING id",
                (name, email)
            )
            user_id = cur.fetchone()[0]
            conn.commit()
            return user_id
    except Exception as e:
        conn.rollback()
        raise
    finally:
        conn.close()

# READ
def get_users():
    conn = get_connection()
    try:
        with conn.cursor(cursor_factory=RealDictCursor) as cur:
            cur.execute("SELECT * FROM users")
            return cur.fetchall()
    finally:
        conn.close()

# UPDATE
def update_user(user_id, name):
    conn = get_connection()
    try:
        with conn.cursor() as cur:
            cur.execute(
                "UPDATE users SET name = %s WHERE id = %s",
                (name, user_id)
            )
            conn.commit()
            return cur.rowcount
    except Exception as e:
        conn.rollback()
        raise
    finally:
        conn.close()

# DELETE
def delete_user(user_id):
    conn = get_connection()
    try:
        with conn.cursor() as cur:
            cur.execute("DELETE FROM users WHERE id = %s", (user_id,))
            conn.commit()
            return cur.rowcount
    except Exception as e:
        conn.rollback()
        raise
    finally:
        conn.close()

# ===== SQLAlchemy ORM =====
from sqlalchemy import create_engine, Column, Integer, String
from sqlalchemy.orm import declarative_base, Session

Base = declarative_base()
engine = create_engine('postgresql://user:pass@localhost/mydb')

class User(Base):
    __tablename__ = 'users'
    id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True)
    name = Column(String(100), nullable=False)
    email = Column(String(200), unique=True)

Base.metadata.create_all(engine)

# CRUD operations
def create_user_orm(name, email):
    with Session(engine) as session:
        user = User(name=name, email=email)
        session.add(user)
        session.commit()
        return user.id

def get_users_orm():
    with Session(engine) as session:
        return session.query(User).all()

from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI
from langchain.agents import AgentExecutor, create_openai_tools_agent
from langchain.tools import tool
from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate, MessagesPlaceholder

# Define Tools
@tool
def query_database(sql: str) -> str:
    """Execute SQL and return results."""
    import psycopg2
    conn = psycopg2.connect("dbname=mydb user=user password=pass")
    cur = conn.cursor()
    cur.execute(sql)
    results = cur.fetchall()
    conn.close()
    return str(results)

@tool
def calculate(expression: str) -> str:
    """Evaluate math expression."""
    return str(eval(expression))

# Create Agent
llm = ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-4", temperature=0)
tools = [query_database, calculate]

prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages([
    ("system", "You are a data analyst. Use tools to answer."),
    ("human", "{input}"),
    MessagesPlaceholder(variable_name="agent_scratchpad"),
])

agent = create_openai_tools_agent(llm, tools, prompt)
agent_executor = AgentExecutor(agent=agent, tools=tools, verbose=True)

# Execute
result = agent_executor.invoke({
    "input": "What is average salary by department?"
})
print(result["output"])

        user = session.query(User).filter(User.id == user_id).first()
        if user:
            user.name = name
            session.commit()

        user = session.query(User).filter(User.id == user_id).first()
        if user:

text:
OLTP (Online Transaction Processing)
- Row-oriented storage
- Optimized for writes/transactions
- Examples: MySQL, PostgreSQL
- Use case: User signups, orders

OLAP (Online Analytical Processing)
- Columnar storage
- Optimized for reads/aggregations
- Examples: CarbonData, Parquet, BigQuery
- Use case: Reports, dashboards, analytics

title: Extended and Alternative Roadmaps
text:
What: Columnar storage format for Hadoop/Spark ecosystem

Key Features:
- Multi-Dimensional Key (MDK) indexing for fast filtering
- Built-in data compression
- Supports ACID transactions
- Optimized for ad-hoc queries on billions of rows

When to Choose:
- Need sub-second queries on very large tables
- Heavy filtering on multiple dimensions (date, region, product)
- Hadoop/Spark ecosystem integration

Interview Strategy:
"I understand CarbonData's MDK indexing accelerates multi-dimensional 
filters. In my project, I used Parquet with similar principles and 
am ready to adopt CarbonData based on the architecture."

title: Extended and Alternative Roadmaps
text:
Star Schema (Data Warehouse):
- Fact tables: Metrics, measures (sales_amount, quantity)
- Dimension tables: Descriptive attributes (customer, product, date)

Normalization vs Denormalization:
- Normalize for OLTP (reduce redundancy, ensure consistency)
- Denormalize for OLAP (reduce joins, faster reads)

Slowly Changing Dimensions (SCD):
- Type 1: Overwrite old value
- Type 2: Add new row with version/dates
- Type 3: Add new column for previous value
