title: Data is everywhere (you make it right now)
text: Every tap, step and swipe writes a record. A data analyst turns raw records into answers and decisions. A record (row) describes one thing — one customer, one order, one sensor ping.; A field (column) is one kind of fact about that thing — name, amount, timestamp.; Big questions ("why did revenue dip?") are answered from tiny facts.; If it can't be measured and written down, a computer can't count it.

title: What a data analyst actually does
text: A fixed pipeline, every single time: question → data → clean → analyze → show → decide. The question decides everything else — a sharp question saves weeks of work.; Cleaning is usually 50–80% of the effort; plan for it, don't pretend.; The deliverable is a decision, not a chart. Charts are the argument.; If any station lies, the decision lies — that's why every step is checkable.

title: How to use this course (60-second version)
text: Every step follows the same rhythm: read one idea, play the motion, touch the controls, answer one question. Green box = real-life version of the idea. Read it first — it's the anchor.; Play / ▶ buttons = the motion. Always press them once; the animation is the explanation.; Sliders & clicks on the canvas = your turn. Break things on purpose.; Answer the question, read the why, then press Next. One step = one idea, nothing more.

title: Tables: rows are things, columns are facts
text: Almost every system on Earth — banks, Netflix, hospitals — stores data in tables: named columns of facts, one row per thing. Row = record: one customer, one order, one ping.; Column = field: one kind of fact, one type (text / number / date).; Duplicate rows are allowed unless you say otherwise (unique constraint).; Every serious database can be read this way — SQL is the shared language on top.

title: WHERE — keep only the rows you asked for
text: A table answers "everything". A question is almost always about a subset — WHERE is how you name that subset. WHERE runs row by row: pass → keep, fail → drop.; AND is stricter (smaller result); OR is looser (bigger result).; IS NULL tests for missing — = NULL would never work (missing ≠ equal to anything).; Big tables: WHERE is also where performance lives — the engine can skip most rows if you write it well (see indexes).

title: GROUP BY + aggregates — from rows to answers
text: "How much did each city spend?" — GROUP BY piles rows into buckets; aggregates (SUM, AVG, COUNT) give each bucket one number. GROUP BY city → one row per city; the rest must go through SUM/AVG/COUNT/MIN/MAX.; HAVING filters after grouping ("cities with SUM > 100"); WHERE filters rows before.; COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(col) skips missing values — often a data-quality tell.; This one pattern (bucket → summarize) is 80% of business reporting.

title: JOINs — combining two tables on a shared key
text:
A name lives in one table, the address in another. JOINs stitch rows together where a key matches — the single most-used operation in analytics.
INNER: only pairs that match — the default, the safest.; LEFT: keep every left row; unmatched ones get NULLs (great for finding orphans).; RIGHT/FULL: mirror images — keep the other side too. FULL keeps everything on both sides.; CROSS: every row × every row (n×m) — a deliberate explosion, rarely wanted.

title: CTEs & subqueries — answer in stages
text: Hard questions are two easy ones. A CTE (WITH x AS (…)) names the first answer, then the second question builds on it. WITH winners AS (…) = "pretend this table exists"; use it by name afterwards.; CTEs can reference earlier CTEs — a chain of named stages.; Subqueries do the same inside a SELECT/WHERE; CTEs are usually more readable.; Each stage is independently checkable — that's the debugging superpower.

title: Window functions — rank & running totals without collapsing
text: GROUP BY crushes rows into one per bucket. Window functions do the math alongside the rows — each row keeps its identity, plus a computed badge. PARTITION BY = buckets that never merge rows (unlike GROUP BY).; ORDER BY inside OVER() decides the ranking / running order.; row_number (unique), rank (gaps on ties), dense_rank (no gaps) — pick by tie policy.; Running totals + RANK = the tool behind 90% of "leaderboard" dashboards.

title: Indexes & B-trees — why "WHERE id=42" is instant
text:
A table with no index is a stack of papers — every search reads everything. An index is a layered signpost: a few hops, then done.
Linear scan = O(n): 10M rows → up to 10M comparisons.; B-tree search = O(log n): 10M rows → ~24 comparisons, same every time.; Indexes cost space and slow down INSERT/UPDATE (they must be kept in sync).; One index per queried column is not the answer — the optimizer picks; over-indexing backfires.

title: Transactions & ACID — the bank transfer promise
text:
"Move €50 from Ana to Ben" is two writes. If the machine dies between them, money is created or destroyed. A transaction makes that impossible.
Atomic: all-or-nothing — the unit of all-or-nothing is the transaction.; Consistent: every rule (total money is constant) holds before and after.; Isolated: two transfers at once don't see each other's half-states.; Durable: after COMMIT, even a crash can't take the money back.

title: Normalization — don't store the same fact twice
text:
If the department manager's name sits in 200 employee rows, one promotion means 200 edits — and the 199 you forget are now lies.
1NF: one value per cell, no repeating groups.; 2NF: no partial dependence (a fact about the dept must not live in a row keyed by employee+dept).; 3NF: no transitive dependence — dept → manager is a dept fact, store it with the dept.; Foreign keys (dept_id) are the glue: small, typed, unambiguous.

title: Mean, median, mode — three centers, three stories
text: "Average" hides three different ideas. Which one you use changes the story — sometimes on purpose. Mean is a balance point — outliers drag it.; Median is a crowd middle — add any number of outliers, it barely moves.; Mode is the typical case — best for categories (most popular size, color).; Reporting "the average" without saying which is how numbers lie politely.

title: Spread: standard deviation — how wild is the data?
text:
Two waiters average the same tips (€15). One is boringly reliable; the other is a slot machine. The average can't tell them apart — spread can.
σ answers "how surprised should I be?" — small σ = predictable.; Variance = σ² — same information, squared (used inside formulas).; For normal data: ~68% of values within mean±1σ, ~95% within mean±2σ.; IQR (middle 50%) is the robust cousin when outliers distort σ.

title: Distribution shape — click to build it yourself
text: A distribution is just a crowd of numbers, sorted into a skyline. Its shape (center, spread, tails) is the story. Symmetric bell ≈ normal — mean = median, σ does the talking.; Right skew: mean > median (a long right tail drags the mean).; Left skew: mean < median.; Tails = risk: heavy tails mean "what usually happens" hides rare, huge events.

title: Correlation vs causation — the ice-cream trap
text:
Ice-cream sales and shark attacks rise and fall together, r ≈ 0.9. Eating ice cream does not summon sharks. A third thing — summer heat — drives both.
r ranges −1…+1: strength AND direction of a linear link.; r=0.9 says nothing about cause, direction, or a hidden third variable.; Classic confounders: season, population size, "more stores of X" = "more people buying X".; The escape hatches: controlled experiments (A/B tests) or carefully argued mechanisms.

title: Sampling & the law of large numbers
text:
You can't taste the whole ocean — you taste a spoonful. Sampling works when the sample is random, and the bigger the spoonful, the closer it gets to the truth.
Random = every unit has a chance — that's what makes the math honest.; Small samples wobble: with n=10, 8 heads (80%) is normal noise, not a biased coin.; Large samples settle: the band shrinks like 1/√n.; Non-random samples can be wrong at ANY size — the math only rescues randomness.

title: Probability: binomial & Poisson — counting rare events
text:
Probability is just "how often would I see this if the world worked the way I think it does?" Two workhorses: binomial (fixed tries) and Poisson (rare arrivals).
Binomial: fixed n independent tries, each success prob p. The bars always sum to 1.; The binomial peak sits near n·p — "expected value = n × p".; Poisson: counts of rare, independent arrivals in a window; λ = average count.; "Rare × many chances" = surprisingly common: 1% failure × 1,000 requests ≈ 63% chance of ≥1 failure.

title: Confidence intervals & hypothesis testing — "is this real?"
text:
Every measurement is truth + noise. A confidence interval is an honest shrug with bounds: "the effect is in this range, 95 times out of 100."
95% CI: build it 100 times, ~95 will cover the true value. (It's about the method, not one interval.); p < 0.05: "if nothing were real, this result would happen < 5% of the time" → reject the null.; Small n → wide CI → everything is "maybe." Power comes from sample size.; A non-significant result ≠ proof of nothing; it means "not enough evidence".

title: A/B testing — the only clean causation machine
text: Correlation watches; experiment does. Split users randomly, change exactly one thing, and the difference in outcomes is the effect — confounders have no time to sneak in. Random split = the engine that kills confounders. Change ONE variable at a time.; Significant = the observed gap would be this big by luck alone < 5% of the time.; Power: small lift + small n → mostly "no verdict." Bigger n is the only honest fix.; Peeking daily and stopping at the first "significant" inflates false wins (the peeking problem).

title: Variables, types & flow — the recipe of a program
text: A program is a recipe the machine follows in order. A variable is a labelled jar: put a value in, read it out, overwrite it — the label always points at the newest value. Names point at values; x = 5 then x = 7 means x is 7 — the 5 is gone.; Types matter: 5 + "5" is an error in Python; "5" * 3 is "555".; str(), int(), float() convert between types — data work is 50% conversions.; Flow is top-to-bottom; if is the only place the recipe forks.

title: Lists, dicts & sets — three ways to group things
text: A list is an ordered shelf (positions matter). A dict is a phonebook (key → value, order irrelevant). A set is a guest list with no repeats (membership only). List [..]: ordered, indexable, duplicates OK. append O(1); inserting at position 0 is O(n).; Dict {k: v}: key→value, lookup O(1) average (a hash table under the hood).; Set {..}: unique values, "in" check O(1) — the dedup tool of choice.; If you find yourself looping to look for something, you probably need a dict/set instead of a list.

title: Loops & comprehensions — do it to every item
text: Data work is 90% "do this to each row." A loop is the machine's version of "take the next one from the pile." A comprehension is the same idea in one line — the idiom you'll see everywhere. for x in coll: — Python hands you each item; avoid tracking indexes by hand.; Comprehension: [expr for x in coll if cond] = map + filter in one line.; range(n) gives 0…n−1 — the classic off-by-one source: it stops BEFORE n.; Loops transform item by item — the output list grows one item per pass.

title: Functions — named machines with input, body, output
text: A function is a vending machine: hand it an input (coin), it runs a fixed process, hands back an output. The caller never sees (or cares about) the mechanism. def name(params): defines once; name(args) calls any number of times.; Each call gets a FRESH frame — its variables don't leak out (local scope).; return ends the call and hands back exactly one value.; No return = None — a function that only prints or mutates returns nothing.

title: pandas DataFrames — the spreadsheet that obeys
text: pandas is a table in memory with a brain: select columns, filter rows, group, fill gaps — each operation returns a new table you can chain. This is 80% of day-to-day analyst code. A DataFrame = columns of one type + an index. Think "typed table."; df[col] selects, df[cond] filters, df.groupby(col).agg() summarizes.; .dropna() / .fillna() / .drop_duplicates() are the three dirty-data basics.; Operations return NEW frames — the original is untouched until you assign (chain-friendly).

title: NumPy & vectorization — one op on a million items
text: Python loops are slow because every step is a full interpreter round-trip. NumPy pushes the whole operation into optimized C running on the array at once — "vectorization" is why data science lives on NumPy/pandas. import numpy as np; xs = np.array([…]) = a typed, contiguous array.; xs * 2 multiplies EVERY element — no loop visible, C code underneath.; Typical speedup 50–1000× on real-sized data; that's the entire pitch.; pandas is built on NumPy — df.col * 2 gets the same win on tables.

title: EDA: load → clean → explore → visualize → question
text:
Exploratory Data Analysis is the fixed ritual before any modeling: get it in, fix what's broken, look at everything, then let the data ask you questions you didn't think to ask.
EDA output is QUESTIONS, not answers — "why is Lyon's amount 3× Paris's?" is a great EDA result.; The 4 classics to check: missing values, duplicates, outliers, type mix-ups.; Plot EVERY numeric column (histograms) — the first pass catches 80% of the surprises.; EDA is iterative: each question sends you back for a second look.

title: What is ML? Learn the rule from examples, don't write it
text: Classic code: you write the rules, the computer follows them. ML: you show labeled examples, the machine finds a general rule that explains them — and applies it to things it has never seen. A model is a function f(x) → prediction whose INSIDE gets tuned automatically, not hand-written.; Labels (the answers) are the teacher; unlabeled data is the raw material.; Generalization = performing well on NEW data — the only metric that counts.; Every ML project is the same loop: predict → measure error → adjust → repeat.

title: Train / validation / test — never peek at the exam
text:
A model graded on the data it studied from looks brilliant. Graded on data it never saw, reality speaks. The split exists to keep those two numbers honest and separate.
Typical split: ~70–80% train, ~10–15% validation, ~10–15% test — all random, all disjoint.; Tuning on the test = data leakage: you've (indirectly) fitted to it; the reported number inflates.; Train ≫ val accuracy? The model memorized (overfit). Both low? It underfits.; The test set is evidence about the future; spending it on experiments burns the evidence.

title: Linear regression — click to build, and the line chases least error
text:
The simplest model: a straight line y = m·x + b. It's chosen by minimizing the Sum of Squared Errors (SSE) — the total squared distance from every point to the line. Every fancy model later is a generalization of this idea.
SSE = Σ(yᵢ − ŷᵢ)². Squaring makes errors positive, punishes big misses hard, and keeps the math smooth (differentiable).; For a single line there's a formula (normal equations) — but most real models have no formula, hence gradient descent (next step).; Correlation ≠ fit: a line fits the TREND; points can still be far from it (residuals).; Always plot residuals after fitting — if they show a curve, a line was the wrong shape.

title: Gradient descent — walk downhill, one baby step at a time
text:
Most models have no closed-form solution, so the machine iterates: compute the slope of the error at the current point (the gradient), take a step opposite it. Step size = learning rate × slope. That's it — everything else is engineering around this loop.
Step:  w ← w − lr · ∂loss/∂w. The gradient is 'the slope of the error' — pointing uphill, so we go opposite.; Learning rate is THE hyperparameter: too small = glacially slow, too large = oscillates or diverges.; Near the bottom the slope → 0, so steps shrink automatically — the ball settles.; This same loop trains a line, a tree-ensemble, and a 100-billion-parameter LLM. Same math, bigger scale.

title: SGD, momentum & Adam — downhill with personality
text:
Raw gradient descent is brittle: noisy slopes stall it, narrow ravines make it zigzag. Momentum adds inertia (a shopping cart keeps rolling), Adam scales each step by the recent step-history (self-adjusting stride). Race them on the same bumpy curve.
SGD: w ← w − lr·g. Simple, but noise makes it jitter and stall on plateaus.; Momentum: v ← βv − lr·g; w ← w + v. Inertia cancels consistent noise and accelerates through flat stretches.; Adam: momentum + per-parameter stride scaling — robust to noisy gradients; the default for deep learning.; These are 'first-order' methods — they only use the slope. The math is trivial; the behavior is profound.

title: Overfitting — when the model memorizes the noise
text:
More capacity fits the training data better. Past a sweet spot it stops learning the pattern and starts memorizing the noise — training error keeps falling, test error starts rising. The U-curve on the right is the single most important picture in ML.
Underfit (bias): model too simple — both errors high.; Overfit (variance): model too flexible — train error → 0, test error rises.; The sweet spot is where VALIDATION error is minimum — that's how you pick complexity in practice.; Regularization (L1/L2) is a dial that nudges the sweet spot toward simpler models.

title: K-nearest neighbours — classify by the local crowd
text:
The simplest model that isn't a line: to label a new point, look at the K closest labelled points and let the majority vote. There is no training phase at all — the model IS the data.
KNN has no training: prediction = find K nearest, majority vote. Simple, interpretable, and a baseline that always works.; K is a hyperparameter: small K → wiggly, noise-sensitive boundary; large K → smooth, but ignores local structure.; Distance metric matters (Euclidean is the default); features must be scaled the same way or big-scale features dominate.; Cost at prediction time grows with the data (a scan over everything) — the reason for tree/ANN indexes at scale.

title: Decision trees — a flowchart of yes/no questions
text:
The model is a flowchart: each internal node asks one question ("amount > 50?"), each branch answers yes or no, each leaf is a prediction. Questions are chosen to purify the split — Gini impurity is the standard yardstick.
Gini = 2·p·(1−p). A pure node (all one class) has Gini 0; a 50/50 mix has Gini 0.5. Splits maximize the Gini DROP.; Trees are interpretable: every prediction is a chain of human-readable questions — rare in ML.; A single tree overfits (it can grow until every leaf is pure); depth limits and pruning control that.; Trees hate one feature dominating: scale features or they split on the 'biggest' one. They also love thresholds — no distance math.

title: Logistic regression — squeeze a line into a probability
text:
Linear regression predicts numbers; classification needs a decision. Logistic regression runs a line's output through the sigmoid, squashing it into 0…1 — a probability — and you choose where to draw the decision threshold.
p = sigmoid(w·x + b). The sigmoid squashes any real number into (0, 1) — a probability.; The threshold converts probability → decision. Lower it = call more positives (more recall, more false alarms).; Output is calibrated: p = 0.8 means '80% of points like this were class 1 in the training data.'; Coefficients stay interpretable: wᵢ is how much feature i pushes the log-odds up or down.

title: K-means — clustering without any labels
text:
No labels, no teacher — just points and a number K. K-means alternates two moves: (1) every point joins its nearest centroid, (2) each centroid moves to the middle of its members. Repeat until nothing moves. The groups discover themselves.
Input: points + K. That's it — no labels, no features to predict. Output: K groups + centroids.; Each iteration strictly lowers the total within-cluster distance, so it always converges — but possibly to a local minimum (restart with random seeds).; K is a decision: the 'elbow' of the within-cluster-distance curve, or the silhouette score, guides the choice.; K-means finds round, equal-size blobs. Elongated or nested clusters need other tools (DBSCAN, GMM).

title: PCA — rotate the axes to where the data actually spreads
text:
Correlated columns carry the same information twice. Principal Component Analysis rotates the axes so the FIRST axis points along the maximum spread (variance). Most real data is 'long and thin' — so one new axis can hold most of the information, and dimensions can be thrown away.
PC1 = direction of MAXIMUM variance; PC2 = max variance left after PC1, always perpendicular.; 'Variance captured' tells you what 93% means: the projected data explains 93% of total spread.; Dimensionality reduction = keep the top k components, drop the rest — cheaper storage + faster models + less noise.; PCA needs centered (and scaled) features; it's unsupervised — the labels are not used.

title: Cross-validation — rotate the exam across k folds
text:
One train/test split wastes most data for training and gets lucky-or-unlucky by which rows happened to land in the test set. K-fold cross-validation: cut the data into k folds, and take turns letting EACH fold be the exam. Average the k scores — a sturdier estimate that trains on more data every round.
k is usually 5 or 10 — a bias/variance trade-off between the estimate and the compute cost.; Every row is training data k−1 times and test data once — no row is wasted, no row is over-graded.; Use CV on the TRAIN+VAL data; the reserved TEST split still grades the final model once.; '5-fold CV, 81.2% ± 1.4%' is the honest way to report a model's expected accuracy.

title: The confusion matrix — accuracy is not enough
text:
On 95% of a 'rare disease' dataset, the model that always says 'healthy' scores 95% and is worthless. The confusion matrix exposes this: it separates the four outcomes — true positives, false positives, false negatives, true negatives — and from them come precision, recall, and F1.
TP = caught it right · FP = false alarm · FN = missed it · TN = correctly quiet.; Precision = TP/(TP+FP): trust in a positive call. Recall = TP/(TP+FN): coverage of the positives.; F1 = harmonic mean of precision & recall — one number when you need to balance both.; Pick the metric from the COST matrix: spam → precision first; disease screening → recall first.

title: ROC & AUC — one curve for every possible threshold
text:
A good classifier emits PROBABILITIES; the threshold is a policy choice. The ROC curve plots TPR (you caught the real ones) against FPR (you falsely accused the innocent) while sweeping the threshold from strict to loose. The area under that curve (AUC) is the model's skill, threshold-free.
TPR = TP/(TP+FN) — you caught the fires. FPR = FP/(FP+TN) — false alarms per innocent.; Sweep the threshold: every threshold is one (FPR, TPR) point; connect them → the ROC curve.; AUC = 'if I pick one random fire and one random no-fire, the model ranks the fire higher.' AUC 0.8 = 80% of the time.; Calibration matters separately: AUC measures RANKING, not whether 0.8 really means 80%.

title: Ensembles — the committee beats the genius
text:
One strong model is good; a committee of many slightly-wrong models that disagree is better. Random forest = many decision trees on shuffled data, majority vote. Gradient boosting = each new model fixes the previous model's mistakes. The math: if errors are independent, averaging cancels the noise and keeps the signal.
Bagging (random forest): many models on shuffled subsets, independent, average the votes → variance drops.; Boosting: models train SEQUENTIALLY on the previous model's mistakes → bias drops (XGBoost, LightGBM).; Both need DIVERSE members: identical models add no information (they just repeat the same error).; Ensembles are the default winners of table-data competitions — and the workhorse of production ML.

title: Neural networks — stacked weighted sums that can draw curves
text:
One neuron computes a weighted sum plus a non-linearity (a sigmoid squish). Stack layers of them and the composition can approximate ANY boundary — circles, spirals, faces. The network has no special knowledge of 'circles'; that shape EMERGES from the stacked sums.
Neuron:  z = Σ wᵢxᵢ + b, then  a = sigmoid(z). That's the ENTIRE unit — everything else is repetition.; Without the non-linearity, stacking layers collapses to one big linear layer — the squish is what lets layers bend the boundary.; Width = how many different 'feature detectors' per layer; depth = how many refinement passes.; Training = the same gradient descent you saw on the ball, applied to thousands of weights at once.

title: Backpropagation — send the blame backwards
text:
Forward pass: predict. Compare with the truth: error. Backward pass: each weight gets a share of the blame — the derivative of the loss with respect to that weight — and nudges against it. This blame-distribution algorithm is backprop, and it is how every modern model learns.
Backprop = the chain rule, automated: ∂loss/∂w for every weight, computed right-to-left in one sweep.; Blame is PROPORTIONAL: a weight on a hot path (large incoming signal) takes more blame than one on a cold one.; The update is identical to gradient descent: w ← w − lr·blame. No new math, just efficient bookkeeping.; Cost: one forward + one backward pass per example — why GPUs (thousands of examples at once) matter.

title: Convolutions — a small filter, slid over the whole image
text:
A CNN's first layer slides a tiny filter (e.g. 3×3) over every position of the image, computing one number per position: 'how much of this pattern is here?' One filter = one feature detector. The output is a new, smaller 'feature map' image where that pattern glows.
One filter = one pattern; a layer stacks many filters (edges in all directions, textures, colors).; The SAME weights are used at every position — 'weight sharing'. Fewer parameters, and the detector works no matter where the pattern is.; Stacking layers composes features: edges → corners → textures → shapes → objects.; The filter 'sees' only its 3×3 window — locality is why CNNs excel at images.

title: Recurrent networks — the same block, run over time
text:
Sequences need memory. An RNN runs ONE block repeatedly: at each time step it reads the new token, updates a hidden state h (a running summary of everything so far), and moves on. The loop IS the architecture — one set of weights, shared across every step.
hₜ = tanh(W·xₜ + U·hₜ₋₁): the new state mixes the new token with the old state. One formula, every step.; The hidden state is the model's working memory — and in a plain RNN it fades (the vanishing gradient problem).; Long-range links ("it" → "cat") are hard: the signal must survive many steps of blending.; Gates (LSTM) and attention (next step) were invented precisely to fix this fading.

title: Attention — let every word look at every word
text:
RNNs compress the past into one fading vector; attention deletes the bottleneck. Every token directly LOOKS at every other token and assigns a weight: 'how much should I copy from you?' Long-range links ('it' → 'cat') are now ONE lookup, no matter the distance.
Attention weight = softmax(Q·Kᵀ/√d): each token's query against every other token's key, normalized to sum to 1.; 'Self'-attention: queries and keys come from the SAME sequence — every token updates itself from the whole context.; Distance no longer costs: 'it'→'cat' is one lookup whether the gap is 6 words or 6000 — this is what made long documents possible.; Multi-head = several attention views in parallel (syntax, coreference, topical…); the transformer = stacked attention + feed-forward layers.

title: LLMs & RAG — the model is the brain, your data is the notebook
text:
A large language model predicts the next token from its context window — brilliant, but it knows NOTHING about your company unless you tell it. RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) closes the gap: embed your documents, search for the ones relevant to the question, paste the top snippets INTO the prompt, and the model answers grounded in your data.
An LLM = next-token prediction at enormous scale; it has no memory between chats and no knowledge of your files.; Embeddings put similar MEANINGS near each other in a vector space — search becomes a nearest-neighbour lookup.; RAG = retrieve top-k snippets → append to prompt → generate. The model only sees what retrieval gives it.; Grounding kills most hallucination on factual questions: the answer has a source you can click. Fresh data needs no retraining.

title: Big-O — counting steps, not seconds
text:
Before any code, the analyst's question: how does the work grow as the data grows? Big-O names the growth shape: O(1) constant, O(log n) halving, O(n) linear, O(n²) quadratic. Two programs that tie at n = 1,000 can differ by YEARS at n = 100,000,000.
Big-O keeps only the dominant term: 3n² + 40n = O(n²). Constants and small terms are noise at scale.; O(log n) = 'halve the search space each step' — binary search, balanced trees.; Rule of thumb: O(n) at 10⁸ ≈ a tenth of a second; O(n²) at 10⁸ ≈ months. Structure choice IS the performance.; Data analysts meet this constantly: nested loops over two big tables are the n² in your pipeline.

title: Arrays — random access is free, insertion is a relay race
text:
An array is one contiguous block of memory. Because every cell is the same size, the machine computes the address of position i in one arithmetic step — that's why reading a[i] is O(1). But everything is glued together: insert at the front and every element must shift.
a[i] = base_address + i·cell_size — one computation, O(1) read.; Append at end: O(1) amortized (occasional resize). Insert at 0: O(n) shifts.; Fixed size (in C) vs dynamic (Python list grows for you) — same address math underneath.; If you're inserting at the front in a loop, you've accidentally built O(n²) — switch to a deque or prepend a marker.

title: Stack vs queue — two ways to hold a line
text:
Both hold items in order; they differ on WHERE you add and remove. Stack: add and remove at the TOP (last in, first out — a pile of plates). Queue: add at the back, remove at the FRONT (first in, first out — a waiting line).
Stack (LIFO): push/pop at top, both O(1). Undo history, browser back, call stack, DFS.; Queue (FIFO): enqueue back, dequeue front, both O(1). Printer jobs, BFS, rate limiters, message systems (Kafka-style).; Peek = look without removing — free on both.; A deque does both ends; Python's collections.deque and JS (push/shift — beware, shift is O(n) on plain arrays).

title: Linked lists — cells that point to their neighbour
text:
A linked list stores items in separate boxes scattered in memory; each box holds a POINTER to the next. No contiguous block, no address math — you reach anything by WALKING from the head, one pointer at a time.
Each node: [value | next]. The head is the only address you keep.; Read the k-th node: O(k) hops. Arrays did that in O(1).; Insert after a known node: O(1) pointer surgery (two rewires). Arrays did that in O(n).; A doubly-linked list adds a prev pointer — remove any node in O(1) once you have it.

title: Hash tables — the O(1) look-up machine
text:
A hash table maps keys to buckets: bucket = hash(key) % size. The hash function scatters similar-looking keys across the table, so a lookup is: compute the bucket, walk the (short) chain there. Average cost: constant, no matter how many keys exist.
hash(key) is a deterministic function: same key → same bucket, every time.; Collisions are normal; resolved by chaining (list per bucket) or open addressing.; Load factor = keys/buckets; rehash (resize + re-insert all) keeps it < ~0.7 → O(1) average.; This is the engine under Python dict, JS object, SQL's join optimization, and your 'is this email a duplicate?' check.

title: Binary search trees — sorted structure, log-depth search
text:
A BST stores sorted data in a tree: left child < node < right child. That one rule means every comparison ELIMINATES HALF the remaining candidates — search, insert, delete all run in O(log n) on a balanced tree. Same rule on sorted input = a degenerate line (O(n)).
Invariant: left < node < right. Search: at each node, half the candidates are gone.; Balanced tree: depth ≈ log₂(n). 1,000,000 nodes → depth ≈ 20.; Sorted inserts destroy balance → depth n → O(n) everywhere. AVL/red-black trees re-balance automatically.; In-order traversal (left, node, right) outputs the keys in sorted order — free.

title: Graphs — BFS rings vs DFS dives
text:
A graph is nodes + edges — the general shape of 'things connected to things.' Two canonical walks: BFS explores in RINGS (nearest neighbours first — shortest paths, Facebook 'degrees of separation'), DFS dives to a LEAF before backtracking (puzzles, cycle detection, topological order).
BFS (queue): visits in distance order → finds the SHORTEST unweighted path.; DFS (stack/recursion): goes deep, backtracks → cycle detection, topological sort, 'is it reachable at all?'.; Both visit every node exactly once; both are O(V + E).; Analyst context: ad-click funnels, dependency graphs, fraud rings — all of it is graph walking.

title: Sorting — bubble the simple, conquer the smart
text:
Sorting is the algorithmic workhorse: 90% of 'find the top/bottom/median' questions are one sort away. Bubble sort is O(n²) — simple, and the reason for its infamy. Quicksort is O(n log n) average — partition around a pivot, recurse on the halves. At n = 1,000,000 the difference is minutes vs milliseconds.
Bubble: adjacent compare-swap, n passes — O(n²). Educational only.; Quicksort: pick pivot, partition (smaller left, bigger right), recurse — O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst on sorted input with bad pivots.; Python's built-in sort is TIMSORT: mergesort + insertion-sort hybrid, O(n log n) guaranteed, stable.; 'Stable' = equal keys keep their original order — it matters when you sort by one column of a table.

title: Searching — linear scan vs binary halving
text:
Unsorted data: scan it (O(n)) — no shortcut exists. Sorted data: halve the search range every step (O(log n)). One value, two orders of magnitude apart at scale: 10⁸ items take 10⁸ checks linearly, or 27 checks binary.
Linear search: O(n), works on ANY data (sorted or not).; Binary search: O(log n), REQUIRES sorted order (or a sorted index).; 27 binary checks cover 10⁸ items; a linear scan takes 10⁸.; SQL 'WHERE x = 5' on a non-indexed column is a linear scan; on an indexed column it's a B-tree lookup (binary-search family).

title: Scale — the moment one machine stops being enough
text:
Every data system hits the same wall: data grows, but one machine's disk, CPU, and memory do not. Two escapes: scale UP (bigger machine — linear money, hard physical ceiling) or scale OUT (many machines sharing the load — the entire field of data engineering).
Scale out = parallelism: work that is independent per row/file/customer divides across machines almost for free.; Scale up = one bigger box: cost grows linearly (and hardware grows super-linearly), and you hit a physical ceiling: one disk, one RAM, one failure.; HDFS, Spark, Kafka all exist to make scale-out routine: chunk it, spread it, aggregate it.; Your data stops fitting in one machine's RAM/disk sooner than you think — that point, not the query speed, is what forces the cluster.

title: HDFS — big files, chopped into blocks, copied 3×
text:
One 768GB file can't live on one disk, and one dead disk must not lose the data. HDFS's answer: split the file into 128MB blocks, scatter the blocks across many machines, and keep THREE copies of every block on different nodes. A node dying is an event, not an incident.
NameNode = metadata only: 'block 7 lives on nodes A, B, C'. It never touches the bytes.; DataNodes = the bytes: each block stored on 3 different nodes (in production: 3 different racks).; 128MB block size: big enough to make reads efficient, small enough to spread load and survive failures.; Client reads a block from the NEAREST replica — parallel reads from several nodes at once.

title: MapReduce — split the work, shuffle the keys, reduce the totals
text:
MapReduce is the pattern the whole field was built on: MAP each input row independently (emit key/value pairs), SHUFFLE (sort+group all pairs by key — the expensive, network-heavy heart), REDUCE (aggregate each key's group). Any computation that is 'sum per group' fits this shape.
MAP is embarrassingly parallel — each row is independent, any machine can do it.; SHUFFLE = the network bottleneck: all pairs with the same key must land on the same reducer (partitioned by hash of key).; REDUCE receives ONE key at a time, already sorted — aggregation is trivial.; This exact shape (emit → group-by → aggregate) is what SQL's GROUP BY, Spark's groupBy, and pandas' groupby all do underneath.

title: Spark — a DAG that keeps intermediates in memory
text:
MapReduce writes EVERY stage's output to disk before the next stage can start. Spark builds the whole job as a DAG of stages and keeps the shuffle data in RAM between them — so a 4-stage job pays the disk tax once instead of three times. For iterative work (machine learning!), the difference is 10–100×.
A 'stage' = work between shuffles. The shuffle boundary is where data changes machines — and in MapReduce, where it hits disk.; Spark's shuffle is in-memory (with disk spill as overflow) — the stage boundary costs milliseconds, not minutes.; Iterative algorithms (gradient descent, k-means) pass over the same data dozens of times: disk-bound MR re-reads it every pass; Spark keeps it resident.; Spark is not 'better SQL' — it's a different execution model: whole-pipeline DAGs vs per-stage disk checkpoints.

title: Kafka — an append-only log, partitioned by design
text:
Kafka's core is not a 'queue' — it's a COMMITTED LOG: messages are appended, never modified, each with an offset. A topic is split into PARTITIONS (independent ordered logs), and messages with the same key always hash to the same partition — which is how you get ordering guarantees at scale.
Append-only + offsets = replay: any consumer can re-read from any offset within the retention window.; Key-based hashing → same key, same partition → per-partition ordering (global ordering is impossible by design).; Consumer GROUP: each partition is consumed by exactly one member — scale consumers to add throughput, not to re-read data.; Consumer LAG = last offset − consumed offset. It is the #1 alert metric for streaming health.

title: Lake vs warehouse — schema-on-read vs schema-on-write
text:
A data LAKE stores files as-is: cheap, flexible, but the schema is only applied when you query (and you pay that cost every query). A data WAREHOUSE validates and structures data AT WRITE time (star schema, types, keys) so queries run on pre-shaped, pre-indexed tables. Modern shops run both: lake for raw flexibility, warehouse for the reporting layer.
Schema-on-read (lake): flexibility + cheap storage; you pay schema work at query time, and mistakes surface late.; Schema-on-write (warehouse): validation at ingest; queries are fast and consistent, but new data shapes need pipeline changes.; Star schema: one wide FACT table (orders, with measure columns) + small DIMENSION tables (customer, product, time) — the shape OLAP engines are built for.; The warehouse is where your dashboards live; the lake is where everything else lives. The pipeline between them is the ETL (later step).

title: The OLAP cube — slice, dice, roll up
text:
Every business question is a cell in a cube: dimensions (TIME, REGION, PRODUCT…) are the axes, and the MEASURE (sales) is the value in each cell. OLAP operations are just ways of grouping the cube: SLICE (fix one dimension to a value), DICE (fix several — one cell), ROLL UP (coarsen an axis: month → quarter), DRILL DOWN (the reverse).
Cell = one combination of dimension values; its value = the measure (SUM, COUNT, AVG…).; SLICE: WHERE time='Q4' — one face. DICE: WHERE time='Q4' AND region='East' — one cell (or a sub-cube).; ROLL UP: GROUP BY quarter instead of month — 12 cells collapse to 4, values pre-aggregated.; Under the hood there is no magic: OLAP is a star schema + materialized aggregations, and the cube is the mental model that makes the SQL obvious.

title: DAX — the formula stays still, the context moves
text:
In DAX (Power BI's formula language) a MEASURE is a formula like SUM(Sales). The formula never changes — what changes is the FILTER CONTEXT: the set of rows the formula is evaluated over. A dashboard filtered to Region=East doesn't run a different formula; it runs the SAME formula over a different slice of the table.
Measure = formula. Filter context = the rows it runs over. Result = f(formula, context).; Contexts intersect (AND): page filter + card filter + slicer all stack on the same table.; CALCULATE() is the tool that deliberately CHANGES the context inside a measure (add/remove filters).; This is why one Power BI measure serves a KPI on the exec page AND a cell in the detail table — the page decides the context.

title: ETL — extract, transform, load (and survive the re-run)
text:
ETL is the daily plumbing: EXTRACT raw rows from sources (CRM, web logs, invoices), TRANSFORM them into one clean shape (fill nulls, parse currencies, drop duplicates), LOAD them into the warehouse. The unglamorous requirement that separates junior from senior pipelines: a re-run must be IDEMPOTENT — running the same day twice must not double the data.
Transform is where trust is BUILT: type coercion, null policy, dedupe keys, validation rules.; 'Dirty data' is not an edge case — it's the normal state of source systems.; Idempotency: load by primary key (upsert) or truncate-and-reload the partition → re-runs are safe.; A pipeline you can't re-run is a pipeline you can't trust — and you WILL need to re-run it.

title: Data quality — trust is a measured thing
text:
A dashboard is only as true as the data behind it. Quality gates make trust explicit: every batch is checked against SLAs (null rate, duplicates, value ranges, freshness) BEFORE it reaches the reporting layer. A gate that fails blocks the load and raises an alert — a dashboard showing a number that failed its checks is a lie with a nice color scheme.
SLAs are numbers: nulls < 1%, dupes = 0, prices > 0, freshness < 24h. 'Looks fine' is not a check.; Gate = hard rule: fail → block the load + alert. The dashboard keeps the last known-good number (labeled as such).; Null rate, dup rate, range, and freshness catch most real-world breakage; add referential checks (FKs) as you grow.; Monitoring quality AFTER load (post-hoc dashboards) is fine for triage — but the gate is what protects the morning meeting.

title: Pick the chart by the question, not by taste
text:
Chart choice is a mapping: each question type has a visual channel that answers it fastest. Compare magnitudes → lengths (bars). Change over time → positions along a line. Parts of a whole → angles/areas (carefully). Distribution → a histogram. Relationship between two numbers → positions in 2D (scatter). Picking the wrong tool doesn't crash — it just makes the answer harder to see.
Compare → bars (length). Trend → line (position on time). Shape → histogram. Relationship → scatter. Part-of-whole → pie ONLY for 2–4 parts that sum to a meaningful total.; Stacked bars = comparison AND composition at once — but non-first segments are read against a moving baseline.; Heatmaps are for the product of two categorical variables (day × region), not for 'pretty'.; If two charts both seem right, ask: what is the FIRST number the reader should take away? Draw the one where that number is a length or

title: What the eye actually compares (channel ranking)
text:
Not every visual encoding is equal. Position and length are read with ±1% accuracy. Angles: only to ~±15°. Areas: ~±30%. 3D volumes: untrustworthy — perspective, occlusion and the ellipse 'lid' all lie. This is why a bar chart beats a pie chart: it uses the eye's best channel, not its worst.
Channel ranking: position/length ≫ angle > area > volume > color for MAGNITUDE. Color is excellent for CATEGORIES (hue = identity, not size).; Pies encode magnitude as ANGLE — the second-worst 2D channel — and 6+ slices makes each angle smaller still.; 3D charts add a third axis that carries no data but corrupts the two that do (decoration with side effects).; The fix is almost always boring: if the eye struggles, replace the encoding — don't add labels (labels are the eye crying for help).

title: Charts that lie — the five tricks (and how to spot them)
text:
A chart can be 100% 'accurate' (every point real, every axis labeled) and still send the reader to a wrong decision. The five classics: (1) truncated y-axis — hide the zero and a 7% change looks like a takeoff; (2) dual axis — two unrelated series on two hidden scales 'correlate'; (3) 3D distortion — volume and perspective inflate the big bars; (4) cherry-picked x-range — show only the months that suit the story; (5) stacked transfer — one series grows inside the stack while the base quietly shrinks.
Truncated y-axis: a line chart with a hidden zero turns a 7% rise into a 'cliff'. Rule: zero-based for magnitudes; truncation only for small changes, clearly labeled.; Dual axis: two series on two independent scales — any two lines can be made to look correlated. Rule: one scale, or don't.; 3D: adds a data-free dimension that inflates tall bars and buries the axis. Rule: it's decoration, not

title: Color systems — categorical, sequential, diverging
text:
Color has exactly three jobs, and mixing them up is the most common 'technical' lie in business charts. CATEGORICAL: distinct hues for distinct things (order means nothing — hue = identity). SEQUENTIAL: light→dark of ONE hue family for ordered magnitude (light = small, dark = big). DIVERGING: two hues meeting at a neutral midpoint around a MEANINGFUL center (zero, average, target). A map of 'deviation from target' painted in a random rainbow is not colorful — it's wrong.
Categorical: distinctness > order. Keep ≤5 hues; beyond that the eye can't keep the mapping, and red–green pairs vanish for ~8% of men.; Sequential: one hue family, light→dark. Magnitude maps, choropleths, heat strips. Never start at full-dark (the light end anchors 'small').; Diverging: two opposite hues, shared neutral center. The center MUST be meaningful (0, mean, target) — diverging around an arbitrary midpoint is a

title: Dashboard layout — the 30-second rule
text:
An executive gives a dashboard about 30 seconds. The eye scans in an F-pattern: top row first, left to right. So the layout encodes importance: HEADLINE KPIs on top (the answer), TREND/CONTEXT in the middle (the story), DETAIL at the bottom (the evidence, for the curious). One dashboard, one audience, one question. Six KPIs that don't answer one question is not a dashboard — it's a wall of numbers.
Top row = the ANSWER (1–3 KPIs tied to the dashboard's one question). If you can't name the question, the dashboard doesn't exist yet.; Middle row = the TREND behind the KPIs (sparklines, funnels). Bottom row = the DETAIL tables for the curious — never in the headline row.; One dashboard ≠ one department's everything. Split by audience: the exec page, the ops page, the debug page.; Density check: if a reader can't say what's 'on fire' in 30 seconds, you have a data dump, not a dashboard.

title: Data storytelling — context first, callouts last
text:
The same chart tells three different stories depending on what surrounds it. Version 1: a naked line — the reader sees 'a line… so what?'. Version 2: add CONTEXT (last year, the plan) — now the reader sees 'we missed plan in September'. Version 3: add the CALLOUT ('summer promo ended') and the ACTION ('re-run the promo Oct–Nov') — now the chart ends in a decision. A chart without a next step is decoration; a story without context is a guess.
Order of the story: CONTEXT (what should we be seeing?) → FINDING (what are we actually seeing?) → CAUSE (why?) → ACTION (what do we do, and what changes when we do?).; Benchmarks do the work: a line against last year and against plan is a different animal from a line alone.; Callouts are sentences, not arrows: 'Sep: promo ended → revenue −18% vs plan' beats a red circle.; Every story needs a next step with a number: 're-run promo, $18k, back to plan

title: The analyst loop — question → data → insight → action
text:
Real analysis is not a line, it's a LOOP. A business question earns a data pull; the data earns an analysis; the analysis earns an insight; the insight earns an ACTION; and the action changes behavior, which creates NEW data, which raises the NEXT question. Analysts who work in a straight line ('crunch → report → done') stop creating value at the report. The loop is what makes the job repeatable.
A question without a DECISION behind it ('how many users?') is trivia, not analysis. 'Should we fix the EU checkout loss?' has money attached — that's a question worth a data pull.; Each beat earns the next: don't pull data until the question has a decision; don't present an insight without an action; don't claim a loop without the feedback arrow.; The feedback beat is the promotion: 'we shipped the fix, here's what the new data says' turns a report into an operating system for the business.; If

title: Anatomy of a portfolio project
text:
A portfolio project is an interview that happens before the interview: a business question with money attached, real (or realistically-messy) data, a method a stranger can follow, ONE insight, an action, and documentation that survives a 10-minute read by someone who doesn't know you. Ten notebook cells of clever code with no decision is not a project — it's a demo. The six stages below are the checklist a hiring manager actually scans.
QUESTION first, with a decision: 'fix the EU checkout loss or accept it' — estimable, time-boxed, money-attached. No decision → no project.; DATA honesty is a feature: 'two dirty joins, 1.4M events, here's how I handled the nulls' beats 'clean synthetic data' every time.; ONE insight, not ten: 'iOS keyboard pushes Pay off-screen' — a single, checkable, dated cause. Ten findings = zero findings.; ACTION with an expected effect: 'fix layout, A/B validate, e

title: Notebook to production — the three gaps
text:
A notebook that runs on your laptop is not a product. Three gaps stand between it and the real job: (1) it must RUN WITHOUT YOU — a schedule, idempotent loads, no human clicks (phase 6's ETL rules); (2) it must FAIL LOUDLY — alerts on null spikes, freshness, breakage, plus auto-retry, so a dead pipeline is discovered in minutes, not at the Monday meeting; (3) it must be CONSUMED — a dashboard or an API where decisions actually happen, not a PDF in a chat channel. Close the gaps in that order and the notebook becomes infrastructure.
Gap 1 · Run without you: a scheduler (cron) + idempotent loads (phase 6) + a versioned repo. 'Works on my machine' is the first gap, and the one that costs the most sleep.; Gap 2 · Fail loudly: quality gates + alerts (phase 6) + auto-retry. A silent dead pipeline is worse than no pipeline — people act on stale numbers.; Gap 3 · Consumed where decisions happen:

title: The 30-second insight — the pyramid (execs read top-down)
text:
Executives process top-down: the recommendation first, then the two or three supporting points, then (if they still care) the evidence. Presenting bottom-up — 'let me walk you through the data' — spends their patience on the evidence before they know what you're asking for. The Pyramid is the shape: RECOMMENDATION at the top (one line), SUPPORTING POINTS below it (2–3), EVIDENCE at the base (the appendix that proves it, for whoever asks). The order you SAY things is the pyramid; the order you BUILT them doesn't matter.
Top line = the RECOMMENDATION with the number: 'double the EU budget — revenue +$40k/wk'. One line, a decision, a stake.; Supporting points: 2–3, each one sentence ('it's all EU-driven', 'payback in 5 months', 'risk is capped at $18k'). No data dumps at this level.; Evidence lives at the BASE and in the APPENDIX: shown only if asked. 'Here's the 40-row table' is a level-3

title: The interview loop — technical, case, take-home
text:
Data interviews run three rounds, each testing a different muscle: (1) TECHNICAL — SQL on a whiteboard (window functions, joins, aggregates) plus pandas and stats intuition; (2) CASE — an unstructured business question ('how would you measure success of a new onboarding flow?') where framing beats fluency: goal → north-star metric + guardrails → hypotheses → data plan, in that order, before any 'data' is touched; (3) TAKE-HOME — a small project judged on depth AND communication: they often grade the one-page summary more heavily than the notebook. The common failure in all three is the same: performing at the level of the question asked, instead of the level of the decision implied.
Technical: confirm edge cases OUT LOUD before coding (duplicates, nulls, ties in ranking, empty tables). Examiners award points for the questions, not just the query.; Case: the first 5 minutes are framing, z

title: Your capstone — the brief (and the stranger test)
text:
The last step of the course is yours. You get a brief, a dataset, and a decision — and you run the whole course against it: the question earns the data (p1), the data earns the analysis (p2, p3), the analysis earns the insight (p4 where a model is honest), the insight earns the story (p7), and the story earns the ship (p8: A/B, docs, the pyramid email). The success criterion is the STRANGER TEST: a person who knows nothing about the project can state the question, your one insight, and the decision — in 10 minutes, unaided. Pass that and you have the first real artifact of a data career.
A brief is worth its decision: all three below have money, a deadline, and a stakeholder who has to DO something with the answer.; The roadmap is the course in miniature: SQL (p1) → stats/EDA (p2, p3) → a model only where it's honest (p4) → story + dashboard (p7) → A/B + pyramid communication (p8).; Scop

What is a Shell?
Think of the shell as a translator between you and the operating system. You type a command in English-like syntax, the shell translates it, the kernel executes it, and the result comes back to your screen.

Ubuntu uses bash (Bourne Again Shell) by default.

The Prompt Explained
text

username@hostname:current_directory$
Symbol	Meaning
$	You are a regular user
#	You are root (superuser)
~	Shortcut meaning your home directory
Example prompt:

text

john@ubuntu:~$        ← john is logged in, currently in home directory
root@ubuntu:/etc#     ← root user, currently in /etc directory

Bash

echo "text or variable"

Bash

echo "Hello World"
# Output: Hello World

# Output: /home/john

echo $USER
# Output: john

echo "Today is: $(date)"
# Output: Today is: Mon Jan 15 10:30:00 UTC 2024

Checking the value of a variable

title: Glossary
text: 0 terms× DA Camp · Visual Crash Course — 79 interactive steps · Esc to close✕ Close VCCVisual Crash Course

title: The mutable default argument
blurb: The default is built once, at definition time, and every call that omits the argument shares it.

title: Shallow copy versus deep copy
blurb: A slice copies the outer list and shares every nested object inside it.

title: Closures capture the variable, not the value
blurb: Every lambda made in the loop closes over the same name, so all three see its final value.

title: A generator is lazy
blurb: Nothing runs until you pull. The function resumes where it left off, keeping its frame alive.

title: Recursion and the call stack
blurb: Each call gets its own frame. Watch the stack grow, then unwind as the returns come back.

title: Grouping rows into a dict
blurb: The split-apply-combine you write by hand before you ever reach for pandas.

title: try / except / else / finally
blurb: Four clauses, and the two that people get wrong under questioning.

title: Inheritance, super and the MRO
blurb: super() walks the instance's MRO, not the class's own parent.

title: Why join beats += in a loop
blurb: Strings are immutable, so each += allocates a new object and copies.

title: Passing a list to a function
blurb: The reference is passed by value: mutation is visible, rebinding is not.

title: Java is pass-by-value, always
blurb: The reference is copied. Mutating through the copy is visible to the caller; rebinding the copy is not.

title: == versus equals, and the string pool
blurb: Literals are interned into one shared object. new String() is not, and a concatenation built in a loop is not either.

title: The Integer cache, and why == lies
blurb: Boxed values from −128 to 127 come from a shared cache. Above that, every box is a new object.

title: Overriding is dynamic, static methods are not
blurb: Instance methods dispatch on the runtime type. Static methods bind at compile time to the declared type.

title: What finally does to a return
blurb: The return value is captured before finally runs. A return inside finally replaces it — and swallows exceptions.

title: try-with-resources closes in reverse
blurb: Three resources open in order and close in the opposite order, before catch and before finally.

RIGHT JOIN     = All rows from RIGHT + matches from LEFT

title: GTS_DOC
text:
-- 1. ROW_NUMBER: unique sequential number
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY city ORDER BY amount DESC)

-- 2. RANK / DENSE_RANK: ranking with ties
RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC)        -- Ties skip numbers (1,2,2,4)
DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC)  -- Ties don't skip (1,2,2,3)

-- 3. LAG / LEAD: access previous/next row
LAG(amount, 1) OVER (ORDER BY order_date)   -- Previous order amount
LEAD(amount, 1) OVER (ORDER BY order_date)  -- Next order amount

-- 4. RUNNING SUM / AVG
SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY order_date ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING)

-- 5. NTILE: split into buckets
NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY amount)   -- Quartiles

title: GTS_DOC
text:
WITH first_orders AS (
    SELECT cust_id,
           MIN(order_date) AS first_order_month,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY cust_id ORDER BY order_date) AS rn
    FROM orders
)
SELECT cust_id, order_date, first_order_month,
       DATEDIFF(month, first_order_month, order_date) AS months_since_first
FROM orders o
JOIN first_orders f ON o.cust_id = f.cust_id AND f.rn = 1;

title: Binary search — logarithmic lookup
text:
def binary_search(a, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(a) - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if a[mid] == target: return mid
        if a[mid] < target: lo = mid + 1
        else: hi = mid - 1
    return -1
print(binary_search([1, 3, 5, 7, 9], 7))
